sources.filename: Labor Code of the Philippines, 2022 Renumbered Edition (DOLE)
sources.notes: Canonical primary source for this module (PD 442 as amended and renumbered per DA No. 01-2015). DOLE.gov.ph sits behind a Cloudflare challenge and returned HTTP 403 to direct retrieval on the access date, so article texts were extracted from the identical DOLE 2016 renumbered edition mirror (src.law.labor-code-2016) and every article cross-checked word-for-word against the Lawphil PD 442 page (src.law.pd442). Renumbering verified: Arts. 58-129 carry the same numbers as the original text; old Arts. 135/248 print as new Arts. 133/259 with bracket notes. The 2016 printing predates RA 11360, so Art. 96 is taken from RA 11360 itself.

sources.publisher: Department of Labor and Employment (via flipbook mirror)
sources.notes: Complete copy of the DOLE renumbered edition (DA No. 01-2015 numbering; reflects amendments through RA 10741). Used to confirm renumbered article numbers, titles, bracket annotations (e.g. ART. 133 [135], ART. 259 [248]), and footnotes (e.g. flex-work advisories, RA 7277 note). sources.filename: Presidential Decree No. 442, as amended (Labor Code, original numbering)
sources.notes: PD 442 text as amended (original numbering). Wording is identical to the renumbered edition for all in-scope articles except the renumbered designations of Arts. 133/259 and the RA 11360 rewrite of Art. 96. Used as the clean-text cross-check for every Labor Code verbatim; known page typos corrected against the amendatory acts (e.g. 'female employees' corrected to RA 6725's 'female employee').

sources.filename: Omnibus Rules to Implement the Labor Code, Book III (Conditions of Employment)
sources.notes: Full text of Book III Rules I-XIV including the RA 6727 wage rules as Rule VII. Used for Rule I (hours worked, waiting/on-call, lectures, meal periods, OT, compulsory OT), Rule IV (holiday pay, absences, holiday-work rates), Rule V (SIL coverage, one-year rule, commutation), and Rule X Secs. 6-13 (payrolls, time records, place of records, false reporting). Cross-checked against the laborlaw.ph library copy; Rule VII here is the RA 6727 version (no facilities rule — facilities doctrine comes from Art. 97(f) and Mabeza).

sources.filename: Republic Act No. 11360 (service charges to covered employees; amends Labor Code Art. 96)
sources.notes: Approved 7 August 2019 (17th Congress consolidation of SB 1299/HB 8784). Current text of Labor Code Art. 96: 100% of collected service charges to covered workers except managerial employees. Verbatim verified against a copy of the Official Gazette printing (115 OG No. 37, Sept. 16, 2019); the enrolled text itself carries two typographical errors ('by law of wage order' and 'increased minimum age'), flagged [sic] in the lesson. Senate, House, and Gazette endpoints returned HTTP 403 on the access date.

sources.filename: Presidential Decree No. 851 (13th-month pay) with 1975 Rules and Supplementary Rules
sources.notes: Promulgated 16 December 1975: Sec. 1 (P1,000 salary ceiling — later removed by MO 28) and Sec. 2 (already-paying exemption). Page also carries the 22 December 1975 Rules (1/12 of basic salary; basic-salary definition; Sec. 3 employer exemptions; Sec. 4 one-month service rule) and Supplementary Rules (piece-rate coverage; OT excluded from basic salary). Current operating rule is the 1987 Revised Guidelines (src.law.rev13th); the 1975 distressed-employer exemption no longer appears there.

sources.filename: Revised Guidelines on the Implementation of the 13th Month Pay Law (16 November 1987)
sources.notes: Secretary Franklin Drilon issuance: MO 28 ceiling removal (all rank-and-file, >=1 month service), exempted employers, rank-and-file test, 1/12 computation and basic-salary inclusions/exclusions, piece-rate and multiple-employer rules, private-school teachers, resigned/separated proration, Dec. 24 deadline, non-credit to regular wage, non-diminution. WARNING: item 5(a) 2nd paragraph (fixed wage + commission computed on total earnings) was declared VOID in Boie-Takeda v. Dela Serna — commissions are excluded from 13th-month basic salary.

sources.filename: Republic Act No. 8972 (Solo Parents' Welfare Act of 2000)
sources.notes: 11th Congress; 17 sections only (Secs. 1-17) — there is NO Sec. 20, so the syllabus citation '(RA 8972, 3, 8, 20)' appears to carry an erroneous '20'. Original Sec. 8 granted 7 working days parental leave after 1 year of service. Substantially amended by RA 11861 (2022): current parental leave is 7 days after 6 months, forfeitable/noncumulative, government + private. Lessons teach the current RA 11861 text and flag the amendment.

sources.filename: Republic Act No. 11861 (Expanded Solo Parents Welfare Act, amending RA 8972)
sources.notes: 18th Congress, dated 4 June 2022. Current law on solo parents: Sec. 3 (amended definitions incl. 'parental leave'), Sec. 4 (categories of solo parent, incl. OFW-family, guardians, 4th-degree relatives, pregnant women), Sec. 7 (amending RA 8972 Sec. 8: forfeitable noncumulative 7-day parental leave after 6 months service). Enrolled-text typos ('exiting laws', 'shills', 'twenty0two') flagged [sic] in the lesson.

sources.filename: Republic Act No. 11210 (105-Day Expanded Maternity Leave Law)
sources.notes: Approved 20 February 2019. Sec. 3 (105 days + 30 optional unpaid + 15 solo-parent; every pregnancy; 60 days for miscarriage/emergency termination), Sec. 4 (public sector), Sec. 5 (private sector: SSS 3-contribution rule, employer advance + SSS reimbursement, salary differential + 4 exemptions), Sec. 6 (allocation of up to 7 days to father/alternate caregiver, over and above RA 8187; reversion on death/incapacity). Sec. 6 included though the syllabus cites only Secs. 3-5 because it completes the Sec. 5 benefit.

sources.filename: Republic Act No. 8187 (Paternity Leave Act of 1996)
sources.notes: Approved 11 June 1996. Sec. 2 (7 days with full pay to married male employees, private + public, first 4 deliveries of legitimate cohabiting spouse; delivery includes miscarriage; notice to employer) and Sec. 3 (statutory definition of paternity leave). Syllabus cites Sec. 3; Sec. 2 is included because it states the grant itself. Unchanged by RA 11210, whose Sec. 6 allocation is expressly 'over and above' RA 8187.

sources.filename: Republic Act No. 9710 (Magna Carta of Women)
sources.notes: Approved 14 August 2009. Only Sec. 18 (Special Leave Benefits for Women: 2 months with full pay based on gross monthly compensation following surgery caused by gynecological disorders, after 6 months aggregate service in last 12 months) is in syllabus scope; the rest of this 66-section Code is outside the module.

sources.filename: Republic Act No. 9262 (Anti-VAWC Act of 2004)
sources.notes: Approved 8 March 2004. Syllabus scope is Sec. 3(c) (Battered Woman Syndrome definition) and Sec. 43 (paid leave up to 10 days in addition to other paid leaves, extendible per protection order; anti-prejudice rule for victims and assisting co-employees). Penal and protection-order provisions are outside the module.

sources.filename: Republic Act No. 9492 (rationalizing celebration of national holidays; amends EO 292 Sec. 26)
sources.notes: Approved 25 July 2007 (holiday economics: Monday-nearest observance; Wednesday->Monday, Sunday->following Monday; movable-holiday proclamation at least 6 months prior; Eidul Adha as ARMM regional holiday). Partly superseded by RA 9849 (Eidul Adha becomes national regular holiday). Enrolled text carries a 'Bataaan' typo, flagged [sic].

sources.filename: Republic Act No. 9849 (Eidul Adha national holiday; amends EO 292 Sec. 26)
sources.notes: Approved 11 December 2009. Sec. 1 declares the 10th day of Zhul Hijja (Eidul Adha) a national holiday; Sec. 2 restates EO 292 Sec. 26 with Eidul Adha in the regular-holiday list. The Sec. 2(c) movable-holiday proviso is grammatically garbled in the enrolled text; the lesson quotes Sec. 1 and the holiday list and cites RA 9492 for the observance mechanics.

sources.filename: Republic Act No. 10966 (December 8 special nonworking holiday; Feast of the Immaculate Conception)
sources.notes: Approved 28 December 2017. Sec. 1 declares December 8 of every year a special nonworking holiday nationwide. (Lawphil passage-date line shows a 'May 2, 20017' typo — immaterial to the two operative sections.)

sources.filename: Executive Order No. 292 (Administrative Code of 1987), Book I, Chapter 7
sources.notes: Promulgated 25 July 1987. Chapter 7 (Secs. 26-28): Sec. 26 lists regular holidays and nationwide special days 'unless otherwise modified by law, order or proclamation' (current text is as amended by RA 9492 and RA 9849); Sec. 27 (local special days by proclamation); Sec. 28 (pretermission: act due on a holiday/special day may be done the next business day). Official Gazette endpoints returned HTTP 403 on the access date.

sources.filename: Presidential Decree No. 1083 (Code of Muslim Personal Laws), Book V, Title I (Muslim Holidays)
sources.notes: Promulgated 4 February 1977. The syllabus's 'Muslim holidays (169-172)' refers to THESE articles (PD 1083 Book V Title I: Art. 169 five official Muslim holidays; Art. 170 provinces/cities of observance; Art. 171 Hijra dating; Art. 172 excusal of Muslim employees), not to Labor Code articles — Labor Code Arts. 169-172 concern employees' compensation and are outside this module. Eidul Fitr and Eidul Adha are now also national regular holidays under EO 292 as amended.

sources.filename: Republic Act No. 6725 (strengthening prohibition on discrimination against women; amends Labor Code Art. 135, now Art. 133)
sources.notes: Approved 12 May 1989. Sec. 1 supplies the current text of Labor Code Art. 133 [135]: ban on sex discrimination plus the two enumerated acts — (a) lesser compensation for work of equal value (the equal-pay rule) and (b) favoring males in promotion/training/scholarships — plus the criminal-liability paragraph. 'Female employee' (singular) confirmed against the Lawphil PD 442 page typo.

sources.filename: Republic Act No. 7277 (Magna Carta for Disabled Persons), Title II, Chapter 1 (Employment)
sources.notes: Approved 24 March 1992. Sec. 5 (equal opportunity for employment: same terms, compensation, benefits as able-bodied; 5% reserve of casual/emergency/contractual posts in DSWD/Health/Education and social-development agencies) and Sec. 7 (PWD apprenticeship eligibility) modernize Labor Code Arts. 78-81. Later amendments RA 9442 (2007) and RA 10754 (2016) touched only privileges/discounts (Secs. 32-33), not the employment chapter — verified against both amendatory acts.

sources.filename: Republic Act No. 9178 (Barangay Micro Business Enterprises Act of 2002)
sources.notes: 2002. Only Sec. 8 is in syllabus scope: registered BMBEs are exempt from the coverage of the Minimum Wage Law (employees keep SSS/healthcare benefits). Cited for the 'exemptions' item under minimum wage alongside Art. 122(e) wage-order exemptions.

sources.filename: Republic Act No. 386 (Civil Code of the Philippines), Book IV (Arts. 1705, 1708)
sources.notes: RA 386 (1949), Book IV. Only two one-sentence articles in scope: Art. 1705 (wages paid in legal currency — cited with Labor Code Art. 102) and Art. 1708 (wages exempt from execution/attachment except debts for food, shelter, clothing, medical attendance — the garnishment item).

sources.filename: 1987 Constitution, Article XIII, Section 3 (Labor)
sources.notes: Ratified 2 February 1987. Syllabus cites pars. 2 and 4: par. 2 (workers entitled to security of tenure, humane conditions of work, and a LIVING WAGE) and par. 4 (right of labor to its just share in the fruits of production; right of enterprises to reasonable returns). Anchors the living-wage principle and Art. 124(a) ('demand for living wages').

sources.filename: DOLE Department Advisory No. 02, Series of 2004 (Implementation of Compressed Workweek Schemes)
sources.publisher: National Administrative Register (via batas.org law library)
sources.notes: Adopted 2 December 2004 (Secretary Patricia Sto. Tomas). Full text retrieved: CWW concept (week < 6 days, 48 hours preserved, workday > 8 hours without OT premium), coverage exclusions (construction, health services, heavy manual labor, OSHS-exceeding exposures), 3 recognition conditions (majority voluntary agreement, OSHS certification where hazardous, DOLE notice), effects (no OT premium to 12 hours/day; 60-minute meals; no diminution; reversion is management prerogative with prior notice). The companion flexible-work advisories (DA 02-2009, DA 04-2010) could not be retrieved (DOLE blocked) and are cited by title only — see coverage notes.

sources.filename: Penaranda v. Baganga Plywood Corp., G.R. No. 159577
sources.publisher: Supreme Court of the Philippines (via Lawphil)
sources.notes: G.R. No. 159577, 3 May 2006, First Division, Panganiban, C.J. Syllabus-named case: shift engineer/foreman held a MEMBER OF THE MANAGERIAL STAFF (not a managerial employee) under Rule I Sec. 2(c) — still outside Title I labor standards, hence no OT or rest-day premium pay. Decision footnotes quote Labor Code Arts. 87 and 93 verbatim (used as an additional cross-check).

sources.filename: David v. Macasio, G.R. No. 195466
sources.publisher: Supreme Court of the Philippines (via Lawphil)
sources.notes: G.R. No. 195466, 2 July 2014, Second Division, Brion, J. Syllabus-named case: pakyaw butcher is an EMPLOYEE (four-fold/control test; pakyaw is a pay method, Art. 97/101), ENTITLED to holiday and SIL pay because he is not field personnel (ejusdem generis; Cebu Institute/Auto Bus/Serrano), but NOT entitled to 13th-month pay (PD 851 Sec. 3(e) task-basis exemption has no field-personnel qualifier). Footnote quotes Art. 101 in full (confirms unlettered single paragraph).

sources.filename: Auto Bus Transport Systems, Inc. v. Bautista, G.R. No. 156367
sources.publisher: Supreme Court of the Philippines (via Lawphil)
sources.notes: G.R. No. 156367, 16 May 2005, Second Division, Chico-Nazario, J. Commission-basis (7% of gross) driver-conductor is NOT field personnel (supervised via inspectors, dispatchers, fixed schedules — BWC advisory opinion quoted) hence ENTITLED to SIL; task/commission phrases read with 'field personnel' by ejusdem generis. Also holds the purely-commission worker excluded from 13th-month pay and states the SIL prescription rule (Art. 291 runs from refusal to commute/pay).

sources.filename: Boie-Takeda Chemicals, Inc. v. Dela Serna, G.R. Nos. 92174 and 102552
sources.publisher: Supreme Court of the Philippines (via Lawphil)
sources.notes: G.R. Nos. 92174 (Boie-Takeda medical representatives) and 102552 (Phil. Fuji Xerox salesmen), consolidated, 10 December 1993, Second Division, Narvasa, C.J. Commissions are NOT part of 'basic salary' for 13th-month computation; Revised Guidelines item 5(a) 2nd paragraph (fixed wage + commission on total earnings) declared VOID for unduly expanding PD 851. Distinguishes Songco ('salary' generic includes commissions; 'basic salary' does not).

sources.filename: Arco Metal Products Co., Inc. v. SAMARM-NAFLU, G.R. No. 170734
sources.publisher: Supreme Court of the Philippines (via Lawphil)
sources.notes: G.R. No. 170734, 14 May 2008, Second Division, Tinga, J. Non-diminution (Art. 100): full 13th-month/bonus/leave encashment paid to 7 short-service employees over 1992-2003 ripened into voluntary company practice — proration ordered withdrawn; 'mistake' defense rejected for want of proof; no fixed minimum number of years for a practice (cites 2-, 3-, 6-year precedents).

sources.filename: Mabeza v. NLRC, G.R. No. 118506
sources.publisher: Supreme Court of the Philippines (via Lawphil)
sources.notes: G.R. No. 118506, 18 April 1997, First Division, Kapunan, J. Facilities doctrine (Art. 97(f)): deductible only upon (1) proof customarily furnished by the trade, (2) voluntary written acceptance, (3) fair and reasonable value. Facilities vs supplements turns on PURPOSE: hotel meals/lodging required for odd-hour availability were supplements (for employer convenience), not deductible facilities (citing States Marine v. Cebu Seamen's, 7 SCRA 294).

sources.filename: Prubankers Association v. Prudential Bank and Trust Co., G.R. No. 131247
sources.publisher: Supreme Court of the Philippines (via Lawphil)
sources.notes: G.R. No. 131247, 25 January 1999, Third Division, Panganiban, J. Wage distortion (Art. 124): four elements (existing hierarchy; significant change at lower level without concomitant higher-level increase; elimination of distinction; same region). Regional wage-order implementation does NOT itself create distortion; inter-regional disparity is RA 6727's design, not an equal-pay violation. 'Establishment' per NWPC Guideline 1-1992: single fixed location.

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 82 (renumbered; same number as original)
provisions.verbatim:
ART. 82. Coverage. The provisions of this Title shall apply to employees in all establishments and undertakings whether for profit or not, but not to government employees, managerial employees, field personnel, members of the family of the employer who are dependent on him for support, domestic helpers, persons in the personal service of another, and workers who are paid by results as determined by the Secretary of Labor in appropriate regulations.

As used herein, "managerial employees" refer to those whose primary duty consists of the management of the establishment in which they are employed or of a department or subdivision thereof, and to other officers or members of the managerial staff.

"Field personnel" shall refer to non-agricultural employees who regularly perform their duties away from the principal place of business or branch office of the employer and whose actual hours of work in the field cannot be determined with reasonable certainty.
provisions.explanation: Art. 82 is the gatekeeper of Title I (Arts. 82-96: hours, rest days, holidays, SIL, service charges). Everyone is covered EXCEPT the seven listed groups — memorize them as a closed list. Two definitions do the heavy lifting: 'managerial employees' (primary duty = management, plus officers/members of managerial staff — Penaranda shows a supervisor can be managerial STAFF even if not a managerial employee) and 'field personnel' (two cumulative tests: away from principal/branch office AND hours not determinable with reasonable certainty). Payroll angle: misclassifying a covered worker as exempt wipes out OT, holiday, and SIL liabilities on paper — exactly what David and Auto Bus punish. Remember: 'paid by results' is NOT a blanket exemption — the IRR (Rules I, IV, V) qualifies it, and task/commission workers get holiday and SIL pay unless they are field personnel.

provisions.citation: Omnibus Rules, Book III, Rule I, Sec. 2
provisions.verbatim:
SECTION 2. Exemption. — The provisions of this Rule shall not apply to the following persons if they qualify for exemption under the conditions set forth herein:

(a) Government employees whether employed by the National Government or any of its political subdivision, including those employed in government-owned and/or controlled corporations;

(b) Managerial employees, if they meet all of the following conditions: (1) Their primary duty consists of the management of the establishment in which they are employed or of a department or sub-division thereof. (2) They customarily and regularly direct the work of two or more employees therein. (3) They have the authority to hire or fire employees of lower rank; or their suggestions and recommendations as to hiring and firing and as to the promotion or any other change of status of other employees, are given particular weight.

(c) Officers or members of a managerial staff if they perform the following duties and responsibilities: (1) The primary duty consists of the performance of work directly related to management policies of their employer; (2) Customarily and regularly exercise discretion and independent judgment; and (3) (i) Regularly and directly assist a proprietor or a managerial employee whose primary duty consists of the management of the establishment in which he is employed or subdivision thereof; or (ii) execute under general supervision work along specialized or technical lines requiring special training, experience, or knowledge; or (iii) execute, under general supervision, special assignments and tasks; and (4) Who do not devote more than 20 percent of their hours worked in a work week to activities which are not directly and closely related to the performance of the work described in paragraphs (1), (2) and (3) above.

(d) Domestic servants and persons in the personal service of another if they perform such services in the employer's home which are usually necessary or desirable for the maintenance and enjoyment thereof, or minister to the personal comfort, convenience, or safety of the employer as well as the members of his employer's household.

(e) Workers who are paid by results, including those who are paid on piece-work, "takay," "pakiao" or task basis, and other non-time work if their output rates are in accordance with the standards prescribed under Section 8, Rule VII, Book Three of these regulations, or where such rates have been fixed by the Secretary of Labor and Employment in accordance with the aforesaid Section.

(f) Non-agricultural field personnel if they regularly perform their duties away from the principal or branch office or place of business of the employer and whose actual hours of work in the field cannot be determined with reasonable certainty.
provisions.explanation: This is the regulation Art. 82 points to ('as determined by the Secretary of Labor'). Exam focus: the THREE-part managerial-employee test (manage + direct 2+ employees + hire/fire authority or weighted recommendations) versus the FOUR-part managerial-STAFF test (management-related work + discretion and independent judgment + assist-a-manager/specialized-work/special-assignments + the 20% cap on unrelated work). Penaranda failed the first test but met the second — and either one takes the worker out of Title I. Practical application: job titles prove nothing; DOLE and the courts test actual duties (David's butcher, Auto Bus's driver). For 'paid by results' (e), the exemption is conditional on proper output rates — it never excuses minimum-wage violations (see Art. 124 last paragraphs).

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 83 (renumbered; same number as original)
provisions.verbatim:
ART. 83. Normal Hours of Work. The normal hours of work of any employee shall not exceed eight (8) hours a day.

Health personnel in cities and municipalities with a population of at least one million (1,000,000) or in hospitals and clinics with a bed capacity of at least one hundred (100) shall hold regular office hours for eight (8) hours a day, for five (5) days a week, exclusive of time for meals, except where the exigencies of the service require that such personnel work for six (6) days or forty-eight (48) hours, in which case, they shall be entitled to an additional compensation of at least thirty percent (30%) of their regular wage for work on the sixth day. For purposes of this Article, "health personnel" shall include resident physicians, nurses, nutritionists, dietitians, pharmacists, social workers, laboratory technicians, paramedical technicians, psychologists, midwives, attendants and all other hospital or clinic personnel.
provisions.explanation: The 8-hour day is the anchor of all premium computations (OT, night differential, holiday pay). Anything beyond 8 hours is overtime by definition — UNLESS a valid compressed workweek (CWW) redefines the normal day. The second paragraph is a special 40-hour week (5 days x 8 hours, meals excluded) for health personnel in big cities (1M+ population) or big facilities (100+ beds); exigency sixth-day work earns at least +30%. Compliance note: government health workers are Title I-exempt and fall under RA 7305 instead (DOLE edition footnote). Remember: 'exclusive of time for meals' — the 60-minute meal break sits outside the 8 hours.

provisions.citation: DOLE Dept. Advisory No. 02, Series of 2004 (Compressed Workweek Schemes)
provisions.verbatim:
For purposes of this Advisory, a CWW scheme is an alternative arrangement whereby the normal workweek is reduced to less than six days but the total number of normal work hours per week shall remain at 48 hours. The normal workday is increased to more than eight hours without corresponding overtime premium. This concept can be adjusted accordingly in cases where the normal workweek of the firm is five days.

[...] DOLE shall recognize CWW schemes adopted in accordance with the following: 1. The CWW scheme is undertaken as a result of an express and voluntary agreement of majority of the covered employees or their duly authorized representatives. This agreement may be expressed through collective bargaining or other legitimate workplace mechanisms of participation such as labor-management councils, employee assemblies or referenda. 2. In firms using substances, chemicals and processes or operating under conditions where there are airborne contaminants, human carcinogens or noise prolonged exposure to which may pose hazards to the employees' health and safety, there must be a certification from an accredited health and safety organization or practitioner or from the firm's safety committee that work beyond eight hours is within threshold limits or tolerable levels of exposure, as set in the OSHS. 3. The employer shall notify DOLE, through the Regional Office having jurisdiction over the workplace, of the adoption of the CWW scheme. [...]

A CWW scheme which complies with the foregoing conditions shall have the following effects: 1. Unless there is a more favorable practice existing in the firm, work beyond eight hours will not be compensable by overtime premium provided the total number of hours worked per day shall not exceed twelve (12) hours. In any case, any work performed beyond 12 hours a day or 48 hours a week shall be subject to overtime premium. 2. Consistent with Article 85 of the Labor Code, employees under a CWW scheme are entitled to meal periods of not less than sixty (60) minutes. [...] 3. Adoption of the CWW scheme shall in no case result in diminution of existing benefits. Reversion to the normal eight-hour workday shall not constitute a diminution of benefits.
provisions.explanation: CWW is the syllabus's 'But see' under normal hours — the lawful way to schedule 10- or 12-hour days without OT premium. Three conditions (majority voluntary agreement + OSHS certification where hazardous + DOLE notice) and three effects (no OT premium up to 12 hours/day; 60-minute meals intact; no diminution — and reverting to 8 hours is NOT diminution). Two hard ceilings survive: work past 12 hours a day or 48 hours a week ALWAYS earns OT premium. Payroll application: a 4x12 schedule pays straight time for all 48 hours; a 13th hour in a day reverts to Art. 87 rates. Remember: without proof of voluntary agreement, the employer owes OT 'as if the CWW scheme did not exist.' Excluded workplaces: construction, health services, heavy manual labor, OSHS-exceeding exposures. The broader flexible-work advisories (DA 02-2009, DA 04-2010) could not be retrieved — cited by title only in the lesson.

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 84 (renumbered; same number as original)
provisions.verbatim:
ART. 84. Hours Worked. Hours worked shall include (a) all time during which an employee is required to be on duty or to be at a prescribed workplace; and (b) all time during which an employee is suffered or permitted to work.

Rest periods of short duration during working hours shall be counted as hours worked.
provisions.explanation: Two alternative tests: (a) required presence (on duty or at a prescribed place) or (b) suffered/permitted work (the employer knew or should have known and let it happen). Either one makes time compensable. 'Suffered or permitted' is the trap: unauthorized-but-known overtime still counts — the remedy is discipline, not non-payment. Short rest periods (Rule I Sec. 7: 5-to-20-minute coffee breaks) are compensable by statute; the 60-minute meal is not. Practical application: payroll controls should capture required early log-ins, through-lunch work, and post-shift completion (Rule I Sec. 4(c)) — all are hours worked if the supervisor knew.

provisions.citation: Omnibus Rules, Book III, Rule I, Secs. 3-7
provisions.verbatim:
SECTION 3. Hours worked. — The following shall be considered as compensable hours worked: (a) All time during which an employee is required to be on duty or to be at the employer's premises or to be at a prescribed work place; and (b) All time during which an employee is suffered or permitted to work.

SECTION 4. Principles in determining hours worked. — The following general principles shall govern in determining whether the time spent by an employee is considered hours worked for purposes of this Rule: (a) All hours are hours worked which the employee is required to give his employer, regardless of whether or not such hours are spent in productive labor or involve physical or mental exertion. (b) An employee need not leave the premises of the work place in order that his rest period shall not be counted, it being enough that he stops working, may rest completely and may leave his work place, to go elsewhere, whether within or outside the premises of his work place. (c) If the work performed was necessary, or it benefited the employer, or the employee could not abandon his work at the end of his normal working hours because he had no replacement, all time spent for such work shall be considered as hours worked, if the work was with the knowledge of his employer or immediate supervisor. (d) The time during which an employee is inactive by reason of interruptions in his work beyond his control shall be considered working time either if the imminence of the resumption of work requires the employee's presence at the place of work or if the interval is too brief to be utilized effectively and gainfully in the employee's own interest.

SECTION 5. Waiting time. — (a) Waiting time spent by an employee shall be considered as working time if waiting is an integral part of his work or the employee is required or engaged by the employer to wait. (b) An employee who is required to remain on call in the employer's premises or so close thereto that he cannot use the time effectively and gainfully for his own purpose shall be considered as working while on call. An employee who is not required to leave word at his home or with company officials where he may be reached is not working while on call.

SECTION 6. Lectures, meetings, training programs. — Attendance at lectures, meetings, training programs, and other similar activities shall not be counted as working time if all of the following conditions are met: (a) Attendance is outside of the employee's regular working hours; (b) Attendance is in fact voluntary; and (c) The employee does not perform any productive work during such attendance.

SECTION 7. Meal and Rest Periods. — Every employer shall give his employees, regardless of sex, not less than one (1) hour time-off for regular meals, except in the following cases when a meal period of not less than twenty (20) minutes may be given by the employer provided that such shorter meal period is credited as compensable hours worked of the employee: (a) Where the work is non-manual work in nature or does not involve strenuous physical exertion; (b) Where the establishment regularly operates not less than sixteen (16) hours a day; (c) In case of actual or impending emergencies or there is urgent work to be performed on machineries, equipment or installations to avoid serious loss which the employer would otherwise suffer; and (d) Where the work is necessary to prevent serious loss of perishable goods. Rest periods or coffee breaks running from five (5) to twenty (20) minutes shall be considered as compensable working time.
provisions.explanation: This is the rule behind nearly every syllabus item on compensable vs non-compensable time. Sec. 4(a): required hours count even if idle (covers power interruptions and idle time together with 4(d): interruption time counts IF presence is required for imminent resumption OR the interval is too brief to use gainfully — if the worker is sent home and free, it does not). Sec. 4(b): a real rest break (stop work, rest completely, free to leave the work place) is not counted. Sec. 4(c): necessary after-hours work with the supervisor's knowledge counts (overtime by sufferance). Sec. 5: waiting counts when integral to the work or the worker is engaged to wait; on-call counts when confined to/near the premises so time cannot be used gainfully (a pager-at-home arrangement with no leave-word requirement does not). Sec. 6: lectures/meetings/training are excluded ONLY if ALL three concur (outside hours + truly voluntary + no productive work) — fail one and the time counts. Sec. 7: shortened 20-minute meals are allowed in the four listed cases but must be CREDITED as compensable; 5-to-20-minute coffee breaks always count. Travel/commuting: ordinary home-to-work travel is not required presence; travel performed as part of the work (required, employer-directed) falls under Sec. 3(a)/4(a). Remember: the pattern is 'required-or-beneficial + known = compensable.'

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 85 (renumbered; same number as original)
provisions.verbatim: ART. 85. Meal Periods. Subject to such regulations as the Secretary of Labor may prescribe, it shall be the duty of every employer to give his employees not less than sixty (60) minutes time-off for their regular meals.
provisions.explanation: The 60-minute meal break is a statutory DUTY of the employer and, as a full hour fully free of work, is the paradigmatic non-compensable period — but it is excluded from the 8 hours only when it is a genuine break (Rule I Sec. 4(b): stop work, rest completely, free to leave the work place). Shortened meals (20+ minutes in the four Rule I Sec. 7 cases) must be credited as compensable hours. Practical application: 'working lunches' at the desk are compensable hours worked, not meal time — a common payroll understatement.

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 86 (renumbered; same number as original)
provisions.verbatim: ART. 86. Night-Shift Differential. Every employee shall be paid a night shift differential of not less than ten percent (10%) of his regular wage for each hour of work performed between ten o'clock in the evening and six o'clock in the morning.
provisions.explanation: Night differential (NSD) is at least +10% of the regular wage for EVERY hour worked in the 10 p.m.-6 a.m. window — it attaches per hour, so a 10 p.m.-6 a.m. shift earns 8 hours of NSD. 'Every employee' means Title I-covered employees; it stacks with overtime and holiday premiums (each premium is computed on its own base). Payroll angle: NSD is part of the wage base for 13th-month purposes ONLY if integrated as basic salary by agreement/practice (Revised Guidelines) — otherwise excluded. Remember the window by the mnemonic '10-to-6, plus-10%.'

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 87 (renumbered; same number as original)
provisions.verbatim: ART. 87. Overtime Work. Work may be performed beyond eight (8) hours a day provided that the employee is paid for the overtime work, an additional compensation equivalent to his regular wage plus at least twenty-five percent (25%) thereof. Work performed beyond eight hours on a holiday or rest day shall be paid an additional compensation equivalent to the rate of the first eight hours on a holiday or rest day plus at least thirty percent (30%) thereof.
provisions.explanation: Two OT formulas: (1) ordinary day: hourly rate x 125% per OT hour; (2) holiday/rest day: (first-8-hours holiday/rest-day hourly rate) x 130% per OT hour. The second formula compounds — e.g., a regular-holiday rest-day OT hour builds on the 260% base. 'May be performed' signals the general rule that OT requires employee consent; compulsory OT exists only under Art. 89 (and Rule I Sec. 10(f) favorable weather). Practical application: compute the hourly rate from the regular wage (monthly wage x 12 / 365 / 8, or the Rule IV Sec. 2 monthly-paid divisor logic), then apply the premium. Remember: CWW days up to 12 hours are NOT overtime — but any CWW excess reverts to this article.

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 88 (renumbered; same number as original)
provisions.verbatim: ART. 88. Undertime Not Offset by Overtime. Undertime work on any particular day shall not be offset by overtime work on any other day. Permission given to the employee to go on leave on some other day of the week shall not exempt the employer from paying the additional compensation required in this Chapter.
provisions.explanation: Each day's OT premium stands alone: Monday's 2-hour undertime cannot cancel Tuesday's 2-hour OT premium, and a mid-week offsetting leave does not erase earned OT pay. This is the anti-averaging rule — weekly-hours averaging (except through a valid CWW) cannot defeat daily OT. Payroll trap: 'flexi-offset' schemes that net undertime against OT within the week violate this article. Remember: undertime affects only the basic wage for that day; overtime always carries its premium.

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 89 (renumbered; same number as original)
provisions.verbatim:
ART. 89. Emergency Overtime Work. Any employee may be required by the employer to perform overtime work in any of the following cases: (a) When the country is at war or when any other national or local emergency has been declared by the National Assembly or the Chief Executive; (b) When it is necessary to prevent loss of life or property or in case of imminent danger to public safety due to an actual or impending emergency in the locality caused by serious accidents, fire, flood, typhoon, earthquake, epidemic, or other disaster or calamity; (c) When there is urgent work to be performed on machines, installations, or equipment, in order to avoid serious loss or damage to the employer or some other cause of similar nature; (d) When the work is necessary to prevent loss or damage to perishable goods; and (e) Where the completion or continuation of the work started before the eighth hour is necessary to prevent serious obstruction or prejudice to the business or operations of the employer.

Any employee required to render overtime work under this Article shall be paid the additional compensation required in this Chapter.
provisions.explanation: The five closed grounds for COMPULSORY overtime: war/declared emergency; loss-of-life/property or public-safety danger; urgent machine/equipment work; perishable goods; and completion of pre-8th-hour work to prevent serious obstruction or prejudice. 'National Assembly' is stale text for Congress (see DOLE edition footnote). Compulsion never means free work — the last paragraph preserves Art. 87 premiums. Rule I Sec. 10 adds a sixth regulatory ground (favorable weather/environmental conditions) and the clincher: outside these grounds, no employee may be made to work beyond 8 hours against his will. Exam point: refusal of OT is insubordination ONLY within Art. 89/Rule I Sec. 10 grounds.

provisions.citation: Omnibus Rules, Book III, Rule I, Secs. 8-10
provisions.verbatim:
SECTION 8. Overtime pay. — Any employee covered by this Rule who is permitted or required to work beyond eight (8) hours on ordinary working days shall be paid an additional compensation for the overtime work in the amount equivalent to his regular wage plus at least twenty-five percent (25%) thereof.

SECTION 9. Premium and overtime pay for holiday and rest day work. — (a) Except employees referred to under Section 2 of this Rule, an employee who is permitted or suffered to work on special holidays or on his designated rest days not falling on regular holidays, shall be paid with an additional compensation as premium pay of not less than thirty percent (30%) of his regular wage. For work performed in excess of eight (8) hours on special holidays and rest days not falling on regular holidays, an employee shall be paid an additional compensation for the overtime work equivalent to his rate for the first eight hours on a special holiday or rest day plus at least thirty percent (30%) thereof. (b) Employees of public utility enterprises as well as those employed in non-profit institutions and organizations shall be entitled to the premium and overtime pay provided herein, unless they are specifically excluded from the coverage of this Rule as provided in Section 2 hereof. (c) The payment of additional compensation for work performed on regular holidays shall be governed by Rule IV, Book Three, of these Rules.

SECTION 10. Compulsory overtime work. — In any of the following cases, an employer may require any of his employees to work beyond eight (8) hours a day, provided that the employee required to render overtime work is paid the additional compensation required by these regulations: (a) When the country is at war or when any other national or local emergency has been declared by Congress or the Chief Executive; (b) When overtime work is necessary to prevent loss of life or property, or in case of imminent danger to public safety due to actual or impending emergency in the locality caused by serious accident, fire, floods, typhoons, earthquake, epidemic or other disaster or calamities; (c) When there is urgent work to be performed on machines, installations, or equipment, in order to avoid serious loss or damage to the employer or some other causes of similar nature; (d) When the work is necessary to prevent loss or damage to perishable goods; (e) When the completion or continuation of work started before the 8th hour is necessary to prevent serious obstruction or prejudice to the business or operations of the employer; or (f) When overtime work is necessary to avail of favorable weather or environmental conditions where performance or quality of work is dependent thereon. In cases not falling within any of these enumerated in this Section, no employee may be made to work beyond eight hours a day against his will.
provisions.explanation: The payroll-implementation companion to Arts. 87-89. Sec. 8 restates the 125% ordinary-OT rate; Sec. 9(a) gives the rest-day/special-holiday premium (130% for the first 8 hours, then that rate x 130% for OT) and expressly covers public-utility and non-profit employees (Sec. 9(b)) — 'non-profit' is not an exemption. Sec. 10 mirrors Art. 89's five grounds (updating 'National Assembly' to 'Congress') and adds ground (f): favorable weather/environmental conditions — the only compulsory-OT basis found solely in the Rules. The closing sentence is the employee's shield: outside these six grounds, overtime against the worker's will is unlawful. Remember: regular-holiday work rates live in Rule IV, not here (Sec. 9(c)).

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 90 (renumbered; same number as original)
provisions.verbatim: ART. 90. Computation of Additional Compensation. For purposes of computing overtime and other additional remuneration as required by this Chapter, the "regular wage" of an employee shall include the cash wage only, without deduction on account of facilities provided by the employer.
provisions.explanation: OT and premium bases use CASH wage only — facilities (meals, lodging) furnished by the employer are neither added to nor deducted from the base. Read with Art. 97(f) (facilities form part of 'wage' for minimum-wage valuation) and Mabeza (facilities deductible from wages only on three conditions): for OT purposes the base stays cash. Practical application: an employee receiving P500/day cash plus P100 meals computes OT on P500, not P600. Remember: 'without deduction' protects the worker both ways — the employer cannot shrink the OT base by the value of facilities.

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 91 (renumbered; same number as original)
provisions.verbatim:
ART. 91. Right to Weekly Rest Day. (a) It shall be the duty of every employer, whether operating for profit or not, to provide each of his employees a rest period of not less than twenty-four (24) consecutive hours after every six (6) consecutive normal work days.

(b) The employer shall determine and schedule the weekly rest day of his employees subject to collective bargaining agreement and to such rules and regulations as the Secretary of Labor and Employment may provide. However, the employer shall respect the preference of employees as to their weekly rest day when such preference is based on religious grounds.
provisions.explanation: The weekly rest formula: 24 consecutive hours after every 6 consecutive normal work days — the '6+1' rhythm. Scheduling is a management prerogative (employer sets the rest day, CBA and DOLE rules permitting), EXCEPT the employer must respect religious-ground preferences (e.g., Saturday Sabbath, Friday observance). 'Whether operating for profit or not' repeats the Rule I Sec. 9(b) point: non-profits owe rest days too. Practical application: shifting schedules (retail, BPO) must still yield one fixed 24-hour rest in every 7-day cycle; compressing the rest below 24 hours violates (a). Remember: Sunday is NOT the default rest day — it is only special when it is the employee's ESTABLISHED rest day (Art. 93(a)).

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 92 (renumbered; same number as original)
provisions.verbatim: ART. 92. When Employer May Require Work on a Rest Day. The employer may require his employees to work on any day: (a) In case of actual or impending emergencies caused by serious accident, fire, flood, typhoon, earthquake, epidemic or other disaster or calamity to prevent loss of life and property, or imminent danger to public safety; (b) In cases of urgent work to be performed on the machinery, equipment, or installation, to avoid serious loss which the employer would otherwise suffer; (c) In the event of abnormal pressure of work due to special circumstances, where the employer cannot ordinarily be expected to resort to other measures; (d) To prevent loss or damage to perishable goods; (e) Where the nature of the work requires continuous operations and the stoppage of work may result in irreparable injury or loss to the employer; and (f) Under other circumstances analogous or similar to the foregoing as determined by the Secretary of Labor and Employment.
provisions.explanation: Six closed grounds for compulsory rest-day work — the rest-day twin of Art. 89, with two distinctive additions: (c) abnormal pressure of work from special circumstances (the classic year-end/seasonal rush ground) and (e) continuous operations where stoppage means irreparable injury or loss (power plants, hospitals, care homes). Outside these grounds, rest-day work needs the employee's consent. Compulsion never cancels premium pay — Art. 93 rates apply to all rest-day work, voluntary or required. Exam point: (f) is a delegation, not a blank check — only the Secretary can declare analogous circumstances.

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 93 (renumbered; same number as original)
provisions.verbatim:
ART. 93. Compensation for Rest Day, Sunday or Holiday Work. (a) Where an employee is made or permitted to work on his scheduled rest day, he shall be paid an additional compensation of at least thirty percent (30%) of his regular wage. An employee shall be entitled to such additional compensation for work performed on Sunday only when it is his established rest day.

(b) When the nature of the work of the employee is such that he has no regular workdays and no regular rest days can be scheduled, he shall be paid an additional compensation of at least thirty percent (30%) of his regular wage for work performed on Sundays and holidays.

(c) Work performed on any special holiday shall be paid an additional compensation of at least thirty percent (30%) of the regular wage of the employee. Where such holiday work falls on the employee's scheduled rest day, he shall be entitled to an additional compensation of at least fifty per cent (50%) of his regular wage.

(d) Where the collective bargaining agreement or other applicable employment contract stipulates the payment of a higher premium pay than that prescribed under this Article, the employer shall pay such higher rate.
provisions.explanation: The premium-pay ladder: rest-day work = 130%; Sunday work = 130% ONLY if Sunday is the established rest day (syllabus 'Sunday' item — working Sundays on a Tuesday-rest schedule earns no premium); no-fixed-schedule workers = 130% for Sunday AND holiday work; special-holiday work = 130%, rising to 150% when the special holiday falls on the scheduled rest day. Paragraph (d) makes CBA/contract rates a floor-raiser, never a ceiling-lowerer. Cross-check: this text was verified against three hosts (DOLE edition, Lawphil, and the Penaranda footnote quotation). Remember the 150%: it is the ONLY 50%-premium in the Code — special day + rest day coincidence.

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 94 (renumbered; same number as original)
provisions.verbatim: ART. 94. Right to Holiday Pay. (a) Every worker shall be paid his regular daily wage during regular holidays, except in retail and service establishments regularly employing less than ten (10) workers; (b) The employer may require an employee to work on any holiday but such employee shall be paid a compensation equivalent to twice his regular rate; and (c) As used in this Article, "holiday" includes: New Year's Day, Maundy Thursday, Good Friday, the ninth of April, the first of May, the twelfth of June, the fourth of July, the thirtieth of November, the twenty-fifth and thirtieth of December and the day designated by law for holding a general election.
provisions.explanation: Holiday pay = 100% of the regular daily wage even when unworked (the great exception to 'no work, no pay'), EXCEPT in retail/service establishments with fewer than 10 workers. Worked regular holidays pay 200% (Rule IV Sec. 4 details the rest-day coincidence: 200% + 30% of 200% = 260%). CRITICAL currency warning: paragraph (c)'s list is INOPERATIVE — it still names July 4th and omits Eidul Fitr/Adha and holiday-economics Monday observance. The current list is EO 292 Sec. 26 AS AMENDED by RA 9492 and RA 9849 (plus RA 10966's December 8 special day). Never quote (c) as the current holiday calendar. David holds pakyaw/task workers entitled to holiday pay unless they are field personnel.

provisions.citation: Omnibus Rules, Book III, Rule IV, Secs. 1-5
provisions.verbatim:
SECTION 1. Coverage. — This rule shall apply to all employees except: (a) Those of the government and any of the political subdivision, including government-owned and controlled corporation; (b) Those of retail and service establishments regularly employing less than ten (10) workers; (c) Domestic helpers and persons in the personal service of another; (d) Managerial employees as defined in Book Three of the Code; (e) Field personnel and other employees whose time and performance is unsupervised by the employer including those who are engaged on task or contract basis, purely commission basis, or those who are paid a fixed amount for performing work irrespective of the time consumed in the performance thereof.

SECTION 2. Status of employees paid by the month. — Employees who are uniformly paid by the month, irrespective of the number of working days therein, with a salary of not less than the statutory or established minimum wage shall be paid for all days in the month whether worked or not. For this purpose, the monthly minimum wage shall not be less than the statutory minimum wage multiplied by 365 days divided by twelve.

SECTION 3. Holiday Pay. — Every employer shall pay his employees their regular daily wage for any worked regular holidays. As used in the rule, the term 'regular holiday' shall exclusively refer to: New Year's Day, Maundy Thursday, Good Friday, the ninth of April, the first of May, the twelfth of June, the last Sunday of August, the thirtieth of November, the twenty-fifth and thirtieth of December. Nationwide special days shall include the first of November and the last day of December. As used in this Rule legal or regular holiday and special holiday shall now be referred to as 'regular holiday' and 'special day', respectively.

SECTION 4. Compensation for holiday work. — Any employee who is permitted or suffered to work on any regular holiday, not exceeding eight (8) hours, shall be paid at least two hundred percent (200%) of his regular daily wage. If the holiday work falls on the scheduled rest day of the employee, he shall be entitled to an additional premium pay of at least 30% of his regular holiday rate of 200% based on his regular wage rate.

SECTION 5. Overtime pay for holiday work. — For work performed in excess of eight hours on a regular holiday, an employee shall be paid an additional compensation for the overtime work equivalent to his rate for the first eight hours on such holiday work plus at least 30% thereof. Where the regular holiday work exceeding eight hours falls on the scheduled rest day of the employee, he shall be paid an additional compensation for the overtime work equivalent to his regular holiday-rest day for the first 8 hours plus 30% thereof. The regular holiday rest day rate of an employee shall consist of 200% of his regular daily wage rate plus 30% thereof.
provisions.explanation: The holiday-pay computation manual. Sec. 1 restates the Art. 82/94 exclusions — and David reads Sec. 1(e)'s task/commission phrase WITH 'field personnel' (ejusdem generis): task-basis workers get holiday pay unless they are field personnel. Sec. 2: monthly-paid employees (paid uniformly regardless of working days, at/above the 365/12 monthly minimum) are already paid for unworked holidays — no separate holiday pay accrues. Sec. 3: note its list is as stale as Art. 94(c) (last Sunday of August, no Eids) — use the EO 292-as-amended calendar. Secs. 4-5 build the rate ladder: worked regular holiday 200%; +rest day 260% (200% + 30% of 200%); OT on regular holiday = first-8-hours rate x 130%; OT on regular-holiday-rest-day = 260% x 130% = 338%. Remember: every holiday-work rate compounds on the rate beneath it.

provisions.citation: Omnibus Rules, Book III, Rule IV, Sec. 6
provisions.verbatim: SECTION 6. Absences. — (a) All covered employees shall be entitled to the benefit provided herein when they are on leave of absence with pay. Employees who are on leave of absence without pay on the day immediately preceding a regular holiday may not be paid the required holiday pay if he has not worked on such regular holiday. (b) Employees shall grant the same percentage of the holiday pay as the benefit granted by competent authority in the form of employee's compensation or social security payment, whichever is higher, if they are not reporting for work while on such benefits. (c) Where the day immediately preceding the holiday is a non-working day in the establishment or the scheduled rest day of the employee, he shall not be deemed to be on leave of absence on that day, in which case he shall be entitled to the holiday pay if he worked on the day immediately preceding the non-working day or rest day.
provisions.explanation: The syllabus 'Absences' item: holiday pay for an UNWORKED regular holiday depends on the day immediately preceding it. On leave WITH pay (or present) the day before = paid. Absent WITHOUT pay the day before = the employer MAY withhold holiday pay — UNLESS the employee actually works the holiday itself (working the holiday always earns the 200% rate). Paragraph (c) saves the worker when the preceding day is itself a non-working/rest day: entitlement then turns on the last actual workday before it. But paragraph (b) is an obvious textual corruption ('Employees shall grant...') — its sense (topping up EC/SSS benefits to the holiday-pay percentage) is noted but not examined. Practical application: HR systems must check the pre-holiday attendance code before releasing unworked-holiday pay. Remember: absence never forfeits pay for a holiday the employee WORKS.

provisions.citation: Omnibus Rules, Book III, Rule IV, Secs. 7-11
provisions.verbatim:
SECTION 7. Temporary or periodic shutdown and temporary cessation of work. — (a) In cases of temporary or periodic shutdown and temporary cessation of work of an establishment, as when a yearly inventory or when the repair or cleaning of machineries and equipment is undertaken, the regular holidays falling within the period shall be compensated in accordance with this Rule. (b) The regular holiday during the cessation of operation of an enterprise due to business reverses as authorized by the Secretary of Labor and Employment may not be paid by the employer.

SECTION 8. Holiday pay of certain employees. — (a) Private school teachers, including faculty members of colleges and universities, may not be paid for the regular holidays during semestral vacations. They shall, however, be paid for the regular holidays during Christmas vacation; (b) Where a covered employee, is paid by results or output, such as payment on piece work, his holiday pay shall not be less than his average daily earnings for the last seven (7) actual working days preceding the regular holiday; Provided, However, that in no case shall the holiday pay be less than the applicable statutory minimum wage rate. (c) Seasonal workers may not be paid the required holiday pay during off-season when they are not at work. (d) Workers who have no regular working days shall be entitled to the benefits provided in this Rule.

SECTION 9. Regular holiday falling on rest days or Sundays. — (a) A regular holiday falling on the employee's rest day shall be compensated accordingly. (b) Where a regular holiday falls on a Sunday, the following day shall be considered a special holiday for purposes of the Labor Code, unless said day is also a regular holiday.

SECTION 10. Successive regular holidays. — Where there are two (2) successive regular holidays, like Holy Thursday and Good Friday, an employee may not be paid for both holidays if he absents himself from work on the day immediately preceding the first holiday, unless he works on the first holiday, in which case he is entitled to his holiday pay on the second holiday.

SECTION 11. Relation to agreements. — Nothing in this Rule shall justify an employer in withdrawing or reducing any benefits, supplements or payments for unworked holidays as provided in existing individual or collective agreement or employer practice or policy.
provisions.explanation: Edge cases examiners love. Sec. 7: shutdown-for-inventory/repair holidays ARE paid; Secretary-authorized business-reverses cessation holidays need not be. Sec. 8: teachers lose semestral-vacation holidays but keep Christmas-vacation ones; piece-rate holiday pay = average of the last 7 actual working days (never below minimum wage); off-season seasonal workers get nothing; no-fixed-schedule workers are covered. Sec. 9: a regular holiday on a rest day is 'compensated accordingly' (the 260% rate via Sec. 4); a regular holiday on Sunday pushes a special-day observance to Monday. Sec. 10: the Maundy-Thursday/Good-Friday rule — absence before the FIRST holiday forfeits BOTH unless the worker works the first (which earns the second). Sec. 11: the Rules never authorize cutting better CBA/company holiday benefits. Remember Sec. 8(b)'s 7-day average — the standard piece-rate exam computation.

provisions.citation: RA 9492, Sec. 1 (amending EO 292, Sec. 26)
provisions.verbatim:
SECTION 1. Section 26, Chapter 7, Book I of Executive Order No. 292, as amended, otherwise known as the Administrative Code of 1987, is hereby amended to read as follows:

"Sec. 26, Regular Holidays and Nationwide Special Days. — (1) Unless otherwise modified by law, and or proclamation, the following regular holidays and special days shall be observed in the country: a) Regular Holidays: New year's Day - January 1; Maundy Thursday - Movable date; Good Friday - Movable date; Eidul Fitr - Movable date; Araw ng Kagitingan (Bataaan [sic] and Corregidor Day) - Monday nearest April 9; Labor Day - Monday nearest May 1; Independence Day - Monday nearest June 12; National Heroes Day - Last Monday of August; Bonifacio Day - Monday nearest November 30; Christmas Day - December 25; Rizal Day - Monday nearest December 30. b) Nationwide Special Holidays: Ninoy Aquino Day - Monday nearest August 21; All Saints Day - November 1; Last Day of the Year - December 31. c) In the event the holiday falls on a Wednesday, the holiday will be observed on the Monday of the week. If the holiday falls on a Sunday, the holiday will be observed on the Monday that follows: Provided, That for movable holidays, the President shall issue a proclamation, at least six months prior to the holiday concerned, the specific date that shall be declared as a nonworking day: Provided, however, The Eidul Adha shall be celebrated as a regional holiday in the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao."
provisions.explanation: The 'holiday economics' law: movable-date regular holidays shift to the nearest Monday (long weekends), Wednesday holidays move to that week's Monday, Sunday holidays to the following Monday. This is the operative holiday calendar together with RA 9849 (which nationalized Eidul Adha — RA 9492's ARMM-only proviso is superseded) and RA 10966 (December 8 special day). Payroll application: the OBSERVED Monday, not the calendar date, triggers holiday-pay and 200%/130% rates. Remember the list mechanics, not just names: 'Monday nearest' for Kagitingan, Labor, Independence, Bonifacio, Rizal, Ninoy Aquino days; fixed dates for New Year, Christmas, All Saints, year-end; movable for Holy Week and the Eids.

provisions.citation: RA 9849, Secs. 1-2 (Eidul Adha; amending EO 292, Sec. 26)
provisions.verbatim:
Section 1. The tenth day of Zhul Hijja, the twelfth month of the Islamic Calendar, is hereby declared as a national holiday for the observance of Eidul Adha. Edul Adha is a tenth day in the month of Hajj or Islamic Pilgrimage to Mecca wherein Mulims [sic] pay homage to Abraham's supreme act of sacrifice and signifies mankind's obedience to God.

Section 2. Section 26, Chapter 7, Book I of Executive Order No. 292 [...] is hereby amended to read as follows: "SEC. 26. Regular Holidays and Nationwide Special Days. - (1) Unless otherwise modified by law, order, or proclamation, the following regular holidays and special days shall be observed in the country: (a) Regular Holidays: New Year's Day - January 1; Maundy Thursday - Movable Date; Good Friday - Movable Date; Eidul Fitr - Movable Date; Eidul Adha - Movable Date; Araw ng Kagitingan (Bataan and Corregidor Day) - Monday nearest April 9; Labor Day - Monday nearest May 1; Independence Day - Monday nearest June 12; National Heroes Day - Last Monday of August; Bonifacio Day - Monday nearest November 30; Christmas Day - December 25; Rizal Day - Monday nearest December 30. [(b)-(c) re-enact RA 9492's special-days list and observance rules — see prov.ra9492-sec1-holidays.]"
provisions.explanation: RA 9849's sole syllabus substance: Eidul Adha (Feast of Sacrifice, 10 Zhul Hijja) joins Eidul Fitr as a NATIONAL regular holiday on movable date — superseding RA 9492's ARMM-only treatment. The Sec. 2 restatement confirms the current 12-regular-holiday roster. Compliance note: because both Eids are movable Islamic-calendar dates, the President fixes the exact Gregorian date yearly ('unless otherwise modified by law, order, or proclamation'). Remember: two Muslim-origin regular holidays on the national calendar — Fitr (end of Ramadan) and Adha (Hajj season).

provisions.citation: RA 10966, Sec. 1 (December 8 special nonworking holiday)
provisions.verbatim: Section 1. December 8 of every year is hereby declared a special nonworking holiday in the entire country to commemorate the Feast of the Immaculate Conception of Mary, the Principal Patroness of the Philippines.
provisions.explanation: A one-line addition to the calendar: December 8 yearly is a NATIONWIDE SPECIAL (nonworking) day — so the Art. 93(c)/Rule I Sec. 9(a) 130% rate (150% on a rest day) applies to work performed, and the 'no work, no pay' principle applies to unworked special days (special days carry no 100%-unworked rule). Remember the classification: regular holidays pay even unworked; special days pay a premium only when worked.

provisions.citation: PD 1083, Arts. 169-172 (Muslim Holidays)
provisions.verbatim:
Article 169. Official Muslim holidays. The following are hereby recognized as legal Muslim holidays: (a) 'Amun Jadid (New Year), which falls on the first day of the first lunar month of Muharram; (b) Maulid-un-Nabi (Birthday of the Prophet Muhammad), which falls on the twelfth day of the third lunar month of Rabi-ul-Awwal; (c) Lailatul Isra Wal Mi'raj (Nocturnal Journey and Ascension of the Prophet Muhammad), which falls on the twenty-seventh day of the seventh lunar month of Rajab; (d) 'Id-ul-Fitr (Hari Raya Pausa), which falls on the first day of the tenth lunar month of Shawwal, commemorating the end of the fasting season; and (e) 'Id-ul-Adha (Hari Raja Haji), which falls on the tenth day of the twelfth lunar month of Dhu 1-Hijja.

Article 170. Provinces and cities where officially observed. (1) Muslim holidays shall be officially observed in the Provinces of Basilan, Lanao del Norte, Lanao del Sur, Maguindanao, North Cotabato, Sultan Kudarat, Sulu, Tawi-Tawi, Zamboanga del Norte and Zamboanga del Sur, and in the Cities of Cotabato, Iligan, Marawi, Pagadian, and Zamboanga and in such other Muslim provinces and cities as may hereafter be created. (2) Upon proclamation by the President of the Philippines, Muslim holidays may also be officially observed in other provinces and cities.

Article 171. Dates of observance. The dates of Muslim holidays shall be determined by the Office of the President of the Philippines in accordance with the Muslim Lunar Calendar (Hijra).

Article 172. Observance of Muslim employees. (1) All Muslim government officials and employees in places other than those enumerated under Article 170 shall also be excused from reporting to office in order that they may be able to observe Muslim holidays. (2) The President of the Philippines may, by proclamation, require private offices, agencies or establishments to excuse their Muslim employees from reporting for work during a Muslim holiday without reduction in their usual compensation.
provisions.explanation: Syllabus trap defused: '(169-172)' is the CODE OF MUSLIM PERSONAL LAWS, not the Labor Code (whose Arts. 169-172 cover employees' compensation — outside this module). Five legal Muslim holidays (Amun Jadid, Maulid-un-Nabi, Lailatul Isra Wal Mi'raj, Id-ul-Fitr, Id-ul-Adha), observed officially in the listed Mindanao provinces/cities (extendable by proclamation), dated by the Hijra calendar. Employment effect: Muslim government personnel elsewhere are excused; PRIVATE Muslim employees are excused without pay loss ONLY upon presidential proclamation. Remember the overlap: Fitr and Adha are additionally NATIONAL regular holidays (EO 292 as amended) — so nationwide, unworked Fitr/Adha days already pay 100% under Art. 94.

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 96, as amended by RA 11360 (2019)
provisions.verbatim:
Art. 96. Service Charges. - All service charges collected by hotels, restaurants and similar establishments shall be distributed completely and equally among the covered workers except managerial employees.

In the event that the minimum wage is increased by law of [sic] wage order, service charges paid to the covered employees shall not be considered in determining the employer's compliance with the increased minimum age [sic].

To facilitate resolution of any dispute between the management and the employees on the distribution of service charges, a grievance mechanism shall be established. If no grievance mechanism is established or if inadequate, the grievance shall be referred to the regional office of the Department of Labor and Employment which has jurisdiction over the workplace for conciliation.

For purposes of this Article, managerial employees refer to any person vested with powers or prerogatives to lay down and execute management policies or hire, transfer, suspend, pay-off, recall, discharge, assign or discipline employees or to effectively recommend such managerial actions.
provisions.explanation: RA 11360 rewrote the economics of service charges: from 85% workers/15% management to ONE HUNDRED PERCENT to covered workers, with management fully cut out ('except managerial employees'). Distribution is 'completely and equally' (the IRR measures this by actual hours/days worked — flagged, not quoted, as outside the syllabus citation). The second paragraph is a minimum-wage firewall: service-charge payouts can NEVER be credited toward minimum-wage compliance after a wage increase — payroll must keep the two streams separate. Disputes go to the firm's grievance mechanism, then DOLE conciliation. 'Managerial employees' here uses the labor-relations definition (policy + hire/fire/recommend powers), matching RA 11360's text. Remember: any pre-2019 material citing the 85/15 split is obsolete law.

provisions.citation: Constitution, Art. XIII, Sec. 3, pars. 2 and 4
provisions.verbatim:
It shall guarantee the rights of all workers to self-organization, collective bargaining and negotiations, and peaceful concerted activities, including the right to strike in accordance with law. They shall be entitled to security of tenure, humane conditions of work, and a living wage. They shall also participate in policy and decision-making processes affecting their rights and benefits as may be provided by law.

[...]

The State shall regulate the relations between workers and employers, recognizing the right of labor to its just share in the fruits of production and the right of enterprises to reasonable returns to investments, and to expansion and growth.
provisions.explanation: The constitutional anchor of the wages topic. Paragraph 2 constitutionalizes the LIVING WAGE (implemented by Art. 124(a)'s 'demand for living wages' criterion and the RTWPB system — never confuse 'living wage' the aspiration with 'minimum wage' the legal floor). Paragraph 4 states the balancing formula every wage answer should echo: labor's just share in the fruits of production AND enterprises' reasonable returns — the same balance Art. 124(h) ('fair return of capital and capacity to pay') operationalizes. Remember: quote par. 2 for living-wage questions, par. 4 for wage-fixing/just-share questions.

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 97(f) (renumbered; same number as original)
provisions.verbatim: ART. 97. Definitions. As used in this Title: [...] (f) "Wage" paid to any employee shall mean the remuneration or earnings, however designated, capable of being expressed in terms of money, whether fixed or ascertained on a time, task, piece, or commission basis, or other method of calculating the same, which is payable by an employer to an employee under a written or unwritten contract of employment for work done or to be done, or for services rendered or to be rendered and includes the fair and reasonable value, as determined by the Secretary of Labor and Employment, of board, lodging, or other facilities customarily furnished by the employer to the employee. "Fair and reasonable value" shall not include any profit to the employer, or to any person affiliated with the employer.
provisions.explanation: The single most-cited wage definition in the module. 'Wage' covers ALL remuneration for work however designated — salary, task pay, piece rates, COMMISSIONS (David, Songco) — so 'wages vs salary' is a false dichotomy under the Code: salary is simply wage paid monthly/periodically. Three extensions matter: (1) 'work done OR TO BE DONE' — advances and guaranteed pay still count as wage; (2) commissions are wages for Title II purposes (but NOT 'basic salary' for 13th-month purposes — Boie-Takeda); (3) facilities (board, lodging) are valued into wages at fair value with NO profit to the employer (Mabeza adds the three deduction conditions). Bonus: a bonus is generally a gratuity (management prerogative), but it becomes demandable wage when promised by contract/CBA or ripened into practice under Art. 100 (Arco Metal). Remember: no-work-no-pay flows from 'for work done or to be done' — pay presupposes the work-for-pay exchange, with statutory exceptions (holiday pay, paid leaves).

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 97(b), (c), (e) (renumbered; same number as original)
provisions.verbatim: ART. 97. Definitions. As used in this Title: [...] (b) "Employer" includes any person acting directly or indirectly in the interest of an employer in relation to an employee and shall include the government and all its branches, subdivisions and instrumentalities, all government-owned or controlled corporations and institutions, as well as non-profit private institutions, or organizations. [...] (c) "Employee" includes any individual employed by an employer. [...] (e) "Employ" includes to suffer or permit to work.
provisions.explanation: The coverage trio for Title II (Wages). 'Employer' sweeps in anyone acting in the employer's interest (supervisors, agents) plus government and non-profits — so wage liability can reach beyond the payroll entity. 'Employ' = 'suffer or permit to work' is the same test as Art. 84(b): tolerated work creates the wage obligation. Practical application: labor-only-contractor workers and suffered volunteers can claim wages from the benefited principal. Remember with Art. 98's exemptions (farm tenancy/leasehold, domestic service, registered cottage-industry homework): Title II covers almost everyone except those three categories.

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 98 (renumbered; same number as original)
provisions.verbatim: ART. 98. Application of Title. This Title shall not apply to farm tenancy or leasehold, domestic service and persons working in their respective homes in needle work or in any cottage industry duly registered in accordance with law.
provisions.explanation: The only three Title II coverage exemptions: (1) farm tenancy/leasehold (agrarian relations, not employment), (2) domestic service (now under the Kasambahay Law, RA 10361 — outside this module), and (3) registered cottage-industry homework/needlework. Note what is NOT exempt: agriculture (farm WORKERS are covered — Art. 97(d) defines agriculture broadly), non-profits, and government (covered as employers under 97(b) for wage purposes, though PD 851 excludes government from 13th-month pay). Exam point: pair Art. 98 (Title II exemptions) against Art. 82 (Title I exemptions) — different lists, different titles; farm workers are Title II-covered but field-personnel rules may exclude some from Title I benefits.

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 100 (renumbered; same number as original)
provisions.verbatim: ART. 100. Prohibition Against Elimination or Diminution of Benefits. Nothing in this Book shall be construed to eliminate or in any way diminish supplements, or other employee benefits being enjoyed at the time of promulgation of this Code.
provisions.explanation: The non-diminution principle: benefits already being enjoyed cannot be withdrawn or reduced by invoking Book III. Jurisprudence extends the shield to voluntarily granted benefits that RIPEN INTO COMPANY PRACTICE — Arco Metal's test: free, voluntary, consistent grants over time (no fixed minimum years; 2-6 years have sufficed), with the employer bearing the burden of proving payment according to law and the 'honest mistake' defense requiring corroboration beyond a bare affidavit. Practical application: before cutting a long-standing allowance, bonus formula, or leave-encashment practice, prove it was never a consistent voluntary grant — otherwise Art. 100 (plus Art. 4's pro-labor construction) voids the cut. Remember its limits: it protects enjoyed benefits; it does not compel granting NEW ones, and CBA/contract interpretation still governs what the benefit is (Arco Metal's first issue).

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 133 [135], lead paragraph and (a) (renumbered; as amended by RA 6725)
provisions.verbatim:
ART. 133. [135] Discrimination Prohibited. It shall be unlawful for any employer to discriminate against any woman employee with respect to terms and conditions of employment solely on account of her sex.

The following are acts of discrimination: (a) Payment of a lesser compensation, including wage, salary or other form of remuneration and fringe benefits, to a female employee as against a male employee, for work of equal value; and (b) Favoring a male employee over a female employee with respect to promotion, training opportunities, study and scholarship grants solely on account of their sexes.
provisions.explanation: The equal-pay-for-equal-work doctrine: paragraph (a) bans paying a woman less than a man — in wage, salary, ANY remuneration or fringe benefits — for work of equal value. Renumbering note (high confusion risk): the DOLE renumbered edition prints this as ART. 133 [135] — old Art. 135 as amended by RA 6725 (1989); the old Art. 133 was maternity-leave benefits, a different, now-superseded article. Paragraph (b) extends the ban to promotion/training/scholarship favoritism. This is sex-based equal pay; Art. 259(e) covers union-membership-based wage discrimination; and Prubankers clarifies that REGION-based wage differences under RA 6727 violate neither. Remember: 'for work of equal value' — the comparison is the work's value, not identical job titles.

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 259(e) [248(e)] (renumbered)
provisions.verbatim: ART. 259. [248] Unfair Labor Practices of Employers. [...] (e) To discriminate in regard to wages, hours of work and other terms and conditions of employment in order to encourage or discourage membership in any labor organization. Nothing in this Code or in any other law shall stop the parties from requiring membership in a recognized collective bargaining agent as a condition for employment, except those employees who are already members of another union at the time of the signing of the collective bargaining agreement. Employees of an appropriate bargaining unit who are not members of the recognized collective bargaining agent may be assessed a reasonable fee equivalent to the dues and other fees paid by members of the recognized collective bargaining agent, if such non-union members accept the benefits under the collective bargaining agreement: Provided, That the individual authorization required under Article 242, paragraph (o) of this Code shall not apply to the non-members of the recognized collective bargaining agent; [...]
provisions.explanation: The second equal-pay anchor: wage (and hours/terms) discrimination designed to encourage or discourage UNION membership is an unfair labor practice. Renumbering note: this is old Art. 248(e) as amended by BP 130 (1981), now printed ART. 259 [248]. The union-security proviso saves valid union-shop clauses (membership in the recognized bargaining agent as a condition of employment, except pre-existing members of another union) and agency fees on benefited non-members. Syllabus placement: this ULP paragraph is cited ONLY for the equal-pay principle — the law of union security and ULPs generally is outside this module. Remember the pair: 133(a) = sex-based pay discrimination; 259(e) = union-based pay discrimination.
