provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 99 (renumbered; same number as original; as amended by RA 6727)
provisions.verbatim: ART. 99. Regional Minimum Wages. The minimum wage rates for agricultural and non-agricultural employees and workers in each and every region of the country shall be those prescribed by the Regional Tripartite Wages and Productivity Boards.
provisions.explanation: One sentence that regionalized Philippine wages: minimum rates are set PER REGION by the RTWPBs — there is no single national minimum wage. Agricultural vs non-agricultural rates may differ, and Boards may further differentiate by industry, province, or locality (Art. 124). Consequence (Prubankers): a Pay Class 4 worker in Cebu may lawfully earn more than a Pay Class 5 worker in Subic — inter-regional disparity is the system's design, not wage distortion or an equal-pay violation. Compliance rule: apply the wage order of the region where the work is performed (RTWPB jurisdiction), verify the current order on the NWPC/RTWPB official postings, and never quote a peso rate as 'national.' Remember: Art. 99 states WHO sets the floor; Arts. 120-124 state HOW.

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 101 (renumbered; same number as original)
provisions.verbatim: ART. 101. Payment by Results. The Secretary of Labor and Employment shall regulate the payment of wages by results, including pakyao, piecework, and other non-time work, in order to ensure the payment of fair and reasonable wage rates, preferably through time and motion studies or in consultation with representatives of workers' and employers' organizations.
provisions.explanation: The Secretary's mandate over non-time pay (pakyaw, piecework, task): rates must be fair and reasonable, set preferably via time-and-motion studies or tripartite consultation. Two floors survive regardless of output: Art. 124 guarantees piece/pakyaw/task workers at least the prescribed wage per 8 hours (proportionate for shorter days), and learner/apprentice/piecework rules (Arts. 61, 75(c), 76, 80) set training-period floors. David confirms pakyaw is a pay METHOD (Art. 97/101) that neither negates employment nor, without field-personnel status, defeats holiday/SIL pay. Commissions are wages under Art. 97(f) — but Boie-Takeda excludes them from 13th-month 'basic salary.' Remember: 'payment by results' regulates HOW wages are computed, never WHETHER minimum standards apply.

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 120 (renumbered; same number as original; per RA 6727)
provisions.verbatim: ART. 120. Creation of National Wages and Productivity Commission. There is hereby created a National Wages and Productivity Commission, hereinafter referred to as the Commission, which shall be attached to the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) for policy and program coordination.
provisions.explanation: Creates the NWPC — the national policy, guideline-setting, review, and appellate body of the wage system — attached to DOLE for coordination. The NWPC does NOT fix regional rates (the RTWPBs do under Art. 122(b)); it sets the guidelines they follow, reviews their levels for consistency with national plans, supervises them technically and administratively, and decides appeals from wage orders (Art. 123: appeal within 10 calendar days of publication; NWPC decides within 60). Remember the division of labor: NWPC = policy + review + appeals; RTWPB = regional rate-fixing + wage orders + exemptions.

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 121 (renumbered; same number as original; per RA 6727)
provisions.verbatim:
ART. 121. Powers and Functions of the Commission. The Commission shall have the following powers and functions: (a) To act as the national consultative and advisory body to the President of the Philippines and Congress on matters relating to wages, incomes and productivity; (b) To formulate policies and guidelines on wages, incomes and productivity improvement at the enterprise, industry and national levels; (c) To prescribe rules and guidelines for the determination of appropriate minimum wage and productivity measures at the regional, provincial, or industry levels; (d) To review regional wage levels set by the Regional Tripartite Wages and Productivity Boards to determine if these are in accordance with prescribed guidelines and national development plans; (e) To undertake studies, researches and surveys necessary for the attainment of its functions and objectives, and to collect and compile data and periodically disseminate information on wages and productivity and other related information, including, but not limited to, employment, cost-of-living, labor costs, investments and returns; (f) To review plans and programs of the Regional Tripartite Wages and Productivity Boards to determine whether these are consistent with national development plans; (g) To exercise technical and administrative supervision over the Regional Tripartite Wages and Productivity Boards; (h) To call, from time to time, a national tripartite conference of representatives of government, workers and employers for the consideration of measures to promote wage rationalization and productivity; and (i) To exercise such powers and functions as may be necessary to implement this Act.

The Commission shall be composed of the Secretary of Labor and Employment as ex-officio chairman, the Director-General of the National Economic and Development Authority (NEDA) as ex-officio vice-chairman, and two (2) members each from workers' and employers' sectors who shall be appointed by the President of the Philippines upon recommendation of the Secretary of Labor and Employment to be made on the basis of the list of nominees submitted by the workers' and employers' sectors, respectively, and who shall serve for a term of five (5) years. The Executive Director of the Commission shall also be a member of the Commission. [...]
provisions.explanation: The NWPC's nine powers reduce to four verbs: ADVISE (President/Congress), PRESCRIBE (guidelines), REVIEW (regional levels and plans), SUPERVISE (the Boards). Composition: Labor Secretary (chair) + NEDA Director-General (vice-chair) + 2 labor + 2 management (5-year terms) + Executive Director — genuine tripartism at the top. The omitted tail (Secretariat ranks and ECC-parity emoluments) is administrative detail outside the syllabus's 'determination' focus. Exam point: wage-order appeals go to the Commission (Art. 123), and appeals do NOT stay the order unless the appellant posts a surety undertaking for the increase — so payroll must implement first and litigate later.

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 122 (renumbered; same number as original; per RA 6727)
provisions.verbatim:
ART. 122. Creation of Regional Tripartite Wages and Productivity Boards. There is hereby created Regional Tripartite Wages and Productivity Boards, hereinafter referred to as Regional Boards, in all regions, including autonomous regions as may be established by law. The Commission shall determine the offices/headquarters of the respective Regional Boards.

The Regional Boards shall have the following powers and functions in their respective territorial jurisdictions: (a) To develop plans, programs and projects relative to wages, incomes and productivity improvement for their respective regions; (b) To determine and fix minimum wage rates applicable in their regions, provinces or industries therein and to issue the corresponding wage orders, subject to guidelines issued by the Commission; (c) To undertake studies, researches, and surveys necessary for the attainment of their functions, objectives and programs, and to collect and compile data on wages, incomes, productivity and other related information and periodically disseminate the same; (d) To coordinate with the other Regional Boards as may be necessary to attain the policy and intention of this Code; (e) To receive, process and act on applications for exemption from prescribed wage rates as may be provided by law or any Wage Order; and (f) To exercise such other powers and functions as may be necessary to carry out their mandate under this Code.

Implementation of the plans, programs, and projects of the Regional Boards referred to in the second paragraph, letter (a) of this Article, shall be through the respective regional offices of the Department of Labor and Employment within their territorial jurisdiction; Provided, however, That the Regional Boards shall have technical supervision over the regional office of the Department of Labor and Employment with respect to the implementation of said plans, programs and projects.

Each Regional Board shall be composed of the Regional Director of the Department of Labor and Employment as chairman, the Regional Directors of the National Economic and Development Authority and the Department of Trade and Industry as vice-chairmen and two (2) members each from workers' and employers' sectors who shall be appointed by the President of the Philippines, upon the recommendation of the Secretary of Labor and Employment, to be made on the basis of the list of nominees submitted by the workers' and employers' sectors, respectively, and who shall serve for a term of five (5) years. Each Regional Board to be headed by its chairman shall be assisted by a Secretariat.
provisions.explanation: The rate-fixers: one RTWPB per region (including autonomous regions), each with six powers — the crown jewel is (b), fixing minimum rates and issuing wage orders within NWPC guidelines. Power (e) is the syllabus 'exemptions' doorway: Boards process exemption applications as the law or the wage order allows (distressed establishments, new businesses, and retail/service shops with 10 or fewer workers are the classic wage-order exemption categories; BMBEs are separately exempt by RA 9178). Composition mirrors the NWPC tripartitely at regional level (DOLE Regional Director chairing; NEDA + DTI directors as vice-chairs; 2 labor + 2 management, 5-year terms). Remember: only the Board of the region where work is performed governs that work — multi-branch payrolls must track each region's order.

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 123 (renumbered; same number as original; per RA 6727)
provisions.verbatim:
ART. 123. Wage Order. Whenever conditions in the region so warrant, the Regional Board shall investigate and study all pertinent facts; and based on the standards and criteria herein prescribed, shall proceed to determine whether a Wage Order should be issued. Any such Wage Order shall take effect after fifteen (15) days from its complete publication in at least one (1) newspaper of general circulation in the region.

In the performance of its wage-determining functions, the Regional Board shall conduct public hearings/consultations, giving notices to employees' and employers' groups, provincial, city and municipal officials and other interested parties.

Any party aggrieved by the Wage Order issued by the Regional Board may appeal such order to the Commission within ten (10) calendar days from the publication of such order. It shall be mandatory for the Commission to decide such appeal within sixty (60) calendar days from the filing thereof.

The filing of the appeal does not stay the order unless the person appealing such order shall file with the Commission, an undertaking with a surety or sureties satisfactory to the Commission for the payment to the employees affected by the order of the corresponding increase, in the event such order is affirmed.
provisions.explanation: How a wage order is born and challenged: fact-finding + public hearings with notice to labor, management, and local officials, then issuance; effectivity 15 days after COMPLETE publication in a regional newspaper of general circulation. Appeal: 10 calendar days from publication to the NWPC, which MUST decide within 60 calendar days of filing — but appeal does NOT stay effectivity unless backed by a satisfactory surety undertaking to pay the increase if affirmed. Compliance consequence: calendar the publication date, implement on day 16, and treat any appeal as non-suspensive unless bonded. Remember the 15-10-60 sequence: 15 to effectivity, 10 to appeal, 60 to decide.

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 124 (renumbered; same number as original; per RA 6727)
provisions.verbatim:
ART. 124. Standards/Criteria for Minimum Wage Fixing. The regional minimum wages to be established by the Regional Board shall be as nearly adequate as is economically feasible to maintain the minimum standards of living necessary for the health, efficiency and general well-being of the employees within the framework of the national economic and social development program. In the determination of such regional minimum wages, the Regional Board shall, among other relevant factors, consider the following: (a) The demand for living wages; (b) Wage adjustment vis-a-vis the consumer price index; (c) The cost of living and changes or increases therein; (d) The needs of workers and their families; (e) The need to induce industries to invest in the countryside; (f) Improvements in standards of living; (g) The prevailing wage levels; (h) Fair return of the capital invested and capacity to pay of employers; (i) Effects on employment generation and family income; and (j) The equitable distribution of income and wealth along the imperatives of economic and social development.

The wages prescribed in accordance with the provisions of this Title shall be the standard prevailing minimum wages in every region. These wages shall include wages varying with industries, provinces or localities if in the judgment of the Regional Board, conditions make such local differentiation proper and necessary to effectuate the purpose of this Title.

Any person, company, corporation, partnership or any other entity engaged in business shall file and register annually with the appropriate Regional Board, Commission and the National Statistics Office, an itemized listing of their labor component, specifying the names of their workers and employees below the managerial level, including learners, apprentices and disabled/handicapped workers who were hired under the terms prescribed in the employment contracts, and their corresponding salaries and wages.

Where the application of any prescribed wage increase by virtue of a law or wage order issued by any Regional Board results in distortions of the wage structure within an establishment, the employer and the union shall negotiate to correct the distortions. Any dispute arising from wage distortions shall be resolved through the grievance procedure under their collective bargaining agreement and, if it remains unresolved, through voluntary arbitration. Unless otherwise agreed by the parties in writing, such dispute shall be decided by the voluntary arbitrators within ten (10) calendar days from the time said dispute was referred to voluntary arbitration.

In cases where there are no collective agreements or recognized labor unions, the employers and workers shall endeavor to correct such distortions. Any dispute arising therefrom shall be settled through the National Conciliation and Mediation Board and, if it remains unresolved after ten (10) calendar days of conciliation, shall be referred to the appropriate branch of the National Labor Relations Commission (NLRC). It shall be mandatory for the NLRC to conduct continuous hearings and decide the dispute within twenty (20) calendar days from the time said dispute is submitted for compulsory arbitration.

The pendency of a dispute arising from a wage distortion shall not in any way delay the applicability of any increase in prescribed wage rates pursuant to the provisions of law or wage order.

As used herein, a wage distortion shall mean a situation where an increase in prescribed wage rates results in the elimination or severe contraction of intentional quantitative differences in wage or salary rates between and among employee groups in an establishment as to effectively obliterate the distinctions embodied in such wage structure based on skills, length of service, or other logical bases of differentiation.

All workers paid by result, including those who are paid on piecework, takay, pakyaw or task basis, shall receive not less than the prescribed wage rates per eight (8) hours of work a day, or a proportion thereof for working less than eight (8) hours.

All recognized learnership and apprenticeship agreements shall be considered automatically modified insofar as their wage clauses are concerned to reflect the prescribed wage rates.
provisions.explanation: The longest in-scope article, carrying four doctrines. (1) The TEN wage-fixing criteria (a)-(j) — memorize the worker-side cluster (living-wage demand, CPI, cost of living, needs, living standards, prevailing levels, employment effects, equitable distribution) against the employer-side pair (countryside investment, fair return/capacity to pay). (2) The wage-DISTORTION machinery: negotiate first; with a union, grievance-then-voluntary-arbitration (10 days); without, NCMB conciliation (10 days) then NLRC compulsory arbitration (20 days, continuous hearings); pendency never delays the increase. Prubankers' four elements (hierarchy; lower-level jump without higher-level match; elimination of distinction; SAME region) plus its holding that regional implementation alone is not distortion. (3) The non-time-worker floor: piece/takay/pakyaw/task workers get at least the prescribed rate per 8 hours (proportionate below 8) — output can never justify sub-minimum pay. (4) Automatic modification of learnership/apprenticeship wage clauses to track new prescribed rates. Plus the annual labor-component reporting duty. Remember: distortion disputes are the ONLY syllabus item routed to voluntary arbitration/NCMB-NLRC — and increases apply while they pend.

provisions.citation: RA 9178, Sec. 8 (BMBE minimum-wage exemption)
provisions.verbatim: Section 8. Exemption from the Coverage of the Minimum Wage Law — The BMBEs shall be exempt from the coverage of the Minimum Wage Law: Provided, That all employees covered under this Act shall be entitled to the same benefits given to any regular employee such as social security and healthcare benefits.
provisions.explanation: The syllabus 'exemptions' item under minimum wage: registered Barangay Micro Business Enterprises are exempt from MINIMUM WAGE rates — but the proviso preserves all other employee benefits (SSS, healthcare, and by extension the rest of labor standards: OT, holiday pay, SIL, 13th month). Registration (Certificate of Authority, now via DTI Negosyo Centers under RA 10644) is the gate: unregistered micro-shops get no exemption. Remember the boundary: BMBE status excuses only the wage floor, never the benefit package.

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 102 (renumbered; same number as original)
provisions.verbatim:
ART. 102. Forms of Payment. No employer shall pay the wages of an employee by means of promissory notes, vouchers, coupons, tokens, tickets, chits, or any object other than legal tender, even when expressly requested by the employee.

Payment of wages by check or money order shall be allowed when such manner of payment is customary on the date of effectivity of this Code, or is necessary because of special circumstances as specified in appropriate regulations to be issued by the Secretary of Labor and Employment or as stipulated in a collective bargaining agreement.
provisions.explanation: Wages must be LEGAL TENDER — scrip, tokens, chits, and company coupons are banned even with the worker's written consent ('even when expressly requested' kills the waiver defense). Checks/money orders are allowed only when customary at effectivity, CBA-stipulated, or justified by Secretary-defined special circumstances. This article does double duty in the syllabus: the 'form' item under payment of wages AND prohibition #1 ('payment by means of any object other than legal tender'). Modern application: ATM/bank payroll is the norm via DOLE's ATM advisory (written consent, nearby facility, no added cost — noted, not quoted, as outside the syllabus citation). Remember: NCC Art. 1705 states the same rule in one sentence — cite both together.

provisions.citation: Civil Code, Art. 1705
provisions.verbatim: Art. 1705. The laborer's wages shall be paid in legal currency.
provisions.explanation: The Civil Code twin of Labor Code Art. 102: wages in legal currency, full stop. Cited in the syllabus alongside Art. 102 for the 'form' of wage payment. Practical pairing: Art. 102 supplies the prohibitions and check exceptions; Art. 1705 supplies the one-line principle to open any exam answer on wage form.

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 103 (renumbered; same number as original)
provisions.verbatim:
ART. 103. Time of Payment. Wages shall be paid at least once every two (2) weeks or twice a month at intervals not exceeding sixteen (16) days. If on account of force majeure or circumstances beyond the employer's control, payment of wages on or within the time herein provided cannot be made, the employer shall pay the wages immediately after such force majeure or circumstances have ceased. No employer shall make payment with less frequency than once a month.

The payment of wages of employees engaged to perform a task which cannot be completed in two (2) weeks shall be subject to the following conditions, in the absence of a collective bargaining agreement or arbitration award: That payments are made at intervals not exceeding sixteen (16) days, in proportion to the amount of work completed; That final settlement is made upon completion of the work.
provisions.explanation: Payday discipline: at least every 2 weeks / twice monthly, never more than 16 days apart — and NEVER less often than monthly (the absolute floor). Force majeure only DEFERS (pay immediately after it ceases), never excuses. Task workers on long tasks get progress payments every <=16 days proportionate to work completed, with final settlement on completion (unless the CBA/arbitration award says otherwise). Payroll application: monthly payroll is lawful; quarterly or 'upon project completion' payroll without progress payments is not. Remember the two numbers: 16 days (interval cap) and 1 month (frequency floor).

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 104 (renumbered; same number as original)
provisions.verbatim: ART. 104. Place of Payment. Payment of wages shall be made at or near the place of undertaking, except as otherwise provided by such regulations as the Secretary of Labor and Employment may prescribe under conditions to ensure greater protection of wages.
provisions.explanation: Wages are paid AT or NEAR the workplace — the rule defeats 'collect your pay at the far-off head office (and spend it at the company store on the way)' abuses. Exceptions exist only through protective Secretary regulations (e.g., the bank/ATM payroll framework: RA 6727 Sec. 7 bank payment for 25+ employee firms near banks, and the DOLE ATM advisory's consent/proximity/no-cost conditions — noted here as context, outside the syllabus citation). Remember: place-of-payment violations pair naturally with Art. 112 (forced purchases at employer stores).

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 105 (renumbered; same number as original)
provisions.verbatim: ART. 105. Direct Payment of Wages. Wages shall be paid directly to the workers to whom they are due, except: (a) In cases of force majeure rendering such payment impossible or under other special circumstances to be determined by the Secretary of Labor and Employment in appropriate regulations, in which case, the worker may be paid through another person under written authority given by the worker for the purpose; or (b) Where the worker has died, in which case, the employer may pay the wages of the deceased worker to the heirs of the latter without the necessity of intestate proceedings. The claimants, if they are all of age, shall execute an affidavit attesting to their relationship to the deceased and the fact that they are his heirs, to the exclusion of all other persons. If any of the heirs is a minor, the affidavit shall be executed on his behalf by his natural guardian or next-of-kin. The affidavit shall be presented to the employer who shall make payment through the Secretary of Labor and Employment or his representative. The representative of the Secretary of Labor and Employment shall act as referee in dividing the amount paid among the heirs. The payment of wages under this Article shall absolve the employer of any further liability with respect to the amount paid.
provisions.explanation: The 'person to pay' rule: DIRECTLY to the worker, with only two exits. (a) Impossibility/special circumstances: payment through an agent needs the worker's WRITTEN authority — verbal 'pakisuyo' arrangements do not discharge the employer. (b) Death: heirs collect WITHOUT intestate proceedings via affidavit (all-of-age heirs attest; minors through guardians), paid THROUGH the Secretary/DOLE representative as referee-divider — and compliant payment ABSOLVES the employer. HR application: never release a deceased worker's last pay to a self-declared relative without the affidavit-and-DOLE channel. Remember: direct payment is the default; every exception is formal (written authority / affidavit / DOLE conduit).

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 112 (renumbered; same number as original)
provisions.verbatim: ART. 112. Non-Interference in Disposal of Wages. No employer shall limit or otherwise interfere with the freedom of any employee to dispose of his wages. He shall not in any manner force, compel, or oblige his employees to purchase merchandise, commodities or other property from any other person, or otherwise make use of any store or services of such employer or any other person.
provisions.explanation: Prohibition #2: the worker's wages are the worker's to spend. Forcing purchases from the company store (or a designated supplier) or compulsory use of employer services violates this article — the classic 'truck system' evil. Consent is no defense where compulsion exists; a genuinely voluntary employee cooperative/store with real choice stands outside the ban. Pairs with Art. 104 (place of payment) and Art. 113 (deductions): the three articles together wall wages off from employer recapture. Remember: 'in any manner' — indirect pressure (quota-linked purchases, supervisor-marketed goods) counts as compulsion.

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 113 (renumbered; same number as original)
provisions.verbatim: ART. 113. Wage Deduction. No employer, in his own behalf or in behalf of any person, shall make any deduction from the wages of his employees, except: (a) In cases where the worker is insured with his consent by the employer, and the deduction is to recompense the employer for the amount paid by him as premium on the insurance; (b) For union dues, in cases where the right of the worker or his union to check-off has been recognized by the employer or authorized in writing by the individual worker concerned; and (c) In cases where the employer is authorized by law or regulations issued by the Secretary of Labor and Employment.
provisions.explanation: Prohibition #3 and the most-cited wage rule in practice: NO deductions except three. (a) Insurance premiums the employer advanced WITH the worker's consent. (b) Union-dues check-off recognized by the employer or individually authorized in writing. (c) The catch-all: deductions authorized BY LAW (SSS, PhilHealth, Pag-IBIG, withholding tax) or by Secretary regulations. Everything else — cash shortages, breakage, unreturned tools, 'voluntary' contributions without the (c) pedigree — needs specific legal authority; Mabeza-style facility deductions additionally need the trade-custom + written-acceptance + fair-value trio. The syllabus cites Art. 113 twice (deductions + withholding) because unlawful withholding (Art. 116) often rides on an unlawful deduction. Remember: when in doubt, the deduction is ILLEGAL unless the employer names its (a), (b), or (c) authority.

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 114 (renumbered; same number as original)
provisions.verbatim: ART. 114. Deposits for Loss or Damage. No employer shall require his worker to make deposits from which deductions shall be made for the reimbursement of loss of or damage to tools, materials, or equipment supplied by the employer, except when the employer is engaged in such trades, occupations or business where the practice of making deductions or requiring deposits is a recognized one, or is necessary or desirable as determined by the Secretary of Labor and Employment in appropriate rules and regulations.
provisions.explanation: Prohibition #4 (with Art. 115): no upfront 'breakage deposits' as wage insurance — EXCEPT in trades where the practice is recognized or the Secretary allows it (e.g., bonded messengers, equipment-intensive contracting). The exception is narrow and trade-specific; a retail chain imposing deposits on all cashiers without that pedigree violates this article. Even where deposits are lawful, Art. 115 gates every peso deducted from them. Remember: Art. 114 bans the REQUIREMENT; Art. 115 polices the DRAW-DOWN.

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 115 (renumbered; same number as original)
provisions.verbatim: ART. 115. Limitations. No deduction from the deposits of an employee for the actual amount of the loss or damage shall be made unless the employee has been heard thereon, and his responsibility has been clearly shown.
provisions.explanation: Two cumulative conditions before touching an Art. 114 deposit: (1) the employee was HEARD (notice + opportunity to explain the loss/damage) and (2) responsibility was CLEARLY SHOWN (more than suspicion — evidence tracing the loss to the worker). Deduction is capped at the ACTUAL amount of loss or damage — no penalties or estimates. Practical application: incident report + worker's explanation + quantified loss memo = the minimum paper trail; skip any leg and the deduction is unlawful. Remember: 'actually heard + clearly shown + actual amount' — the triple lock on deposits.

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 116 (renumbered; same number as original)
provisions.verbatim: ART. 116. Withholding of Wages and Kickbacks Prohibited. It shall be unlawful for any person, directly or indirectly, to withhold any amount from the wages of a worker or induce him to give up any part of his wages by force, stealth, intimidation, threat or by any other means whatsoever without the worker's consent.
provisions.explanation: Prohibition #5: withholding wages or inducing their surrender by force, stealth, intimidation, threat, or ANY other means without consent — 'directly or indirectly' catches supervisors, recruiters, and middlemen, not just the employer. 'Without the worker's consent' is the hinge: genuine, uncoerced consent (e.g., a freely agreed salary loan) stands outside the ban; consent extracted by threat of dismissal does not. Kickbacks (return part of your pay or lose the job) are the archetypal violation. The syllabus pairs Art. 116 with Art. 113 because withholdings usually disguise themselves as deductions — test the authority under 113 first, then the consent under 116. Remember: 'by any other means whatsoever' — the method list is illustrative, not closed.

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 117 (renumbered; same number as original)
provisions.verbatim: ART. 117. Deduction to Ensure Employment. It shall be unlawful to make any deduction from the wages of any employee for the benefit of the employer or his representative or intermediary as consideration of a promise of employment or retention in employment.
provisions.explanation: Prohibition #6: no pay-to-be-hired or pay-to-stay deductions — placement fees, 'goodwill' deductions, or retention kickbacks taken from wages for the employer's (or recruiter's) benefit are unlawful. The evil is the WAGE deduction as the price of the job; legitimate pre-employment costs shouldered by the employer stay with the employer. Distinguish from Art. 116: Art. 117 targets the employment-bargain context specifically (promise of hiring or retention as consideration). Remember: any deduction whose real price is the job itself violates this article regardless of what the payslip calls it.

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 118 (renumbered; same number as original)
provisions.verbatim: ART. 118. Retaliatory Measures. It shall be unlawful for an employer to refuse to pay or reduce the wages and benefits, discharge or in any manner discriminate against any employee who has filed any complaint or instituted any proceeding under this Title or has testified or is about to testify in such proceedings.
provisions.explanation: Prohibition #7: the anti-retaliation shield of Title II — no wage cuts, benefit reductions, dismissal, or any discrimination against workers who complain, sue, testify, or are ABOUT to testify in wage proceedings. 'About to testify' extends protection to the pre-hearing stage (compare Art. 259(f)'s ULP twin for testimony generally). Practical application: any adverse action closely following a DOLE wage complaint bears a presumption of suspicion — document independent just cause meticulously. Remember: the shield covers complaints 'under this Title' (wages) — but parallel protections (Arts. 259(f), 118-read-with-4) make retaliation for any labor-standards complaint perilous.

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 119 (renumbered; same number as original)
provisions.verbatim: ART. 119. False Reporting. It shall be unlawful for any person to make any statement, report, or record filed or kept pursuant to the provisions of this Code knowing such statement, report or record to be false in any material respect.
provisions.explanation: Prohibition #8 (with Art. 128(f) and Rule X Sec. 13): KNOWINGLY false statements, reports, or records under the Code — ghost payrolls, understated hours, fabricated time records. 'Knowing' and 'material' are both required: honest clerical errors are not crimes, but deliberately sanitized records (Mabeza's accountant-prepared summaries, Penaranda-style disputes) are. The enforcement chain: Art. 128(f) empowers the Secretary to REQUIRE employment records; Rule X details payrolls/time records; Art. 119 + Rule X Sec. 13 punish falsifying them. Remember: keep real records — the visitorial power (Art. 128(a)) lets inspectors copy and verify them on the spot.

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 128(a) and (f) (renumbered; same number as original; (b) as amended by RA 7730)
provisions.verbatim:
ART. 128. Visitorial and Enforcement Power. (a) The Secretary of Labor and Employment or his duly authorized representatives, including labor regulation officers, shall have access to employer's records and premises at any time of the day or night whenever work is being undertaken therein, and the right to copy therefrom, to question any employee and investigate any fact, condition or matter which may be necessary to determine violations or which may aid in the enforcement of this Code and of any labor law, wage order or rules and regulations issued pursuant thereto.

[...] (f) The Secretary of Labor and Employment may, by appropriate regulations, require employers to keep and maintain such employment records as may be necessary in aid of his visitorial and enforcement powers under this Code.
provisions.explanation: The enforcement backbone of the prohibitions (paragraphs (b)-(e) on compliance orders, appeals, stoppage, and obstruction are outside the syllabus citation and omitted). Paragraph (a): DOLE access to records AND premises day or night during work, with rights to copy, question, and investigate — no warrant requirement stated; this is the visitorial power routine inspections (like Boie-Takeda's) ride on. Paragraph (f): the records REQUIREMENT power — implemented by Rule X Secs. 6-12 (payrolls, time records, 3-year preservation, PLACE of records) and fenced by Art. 119 + Rule X Sec. 13 (false reporting). Cross-reference note: the 2016 printing's paragraph (b) cites 'Articles 129 and 217' with a footnote that Art. 217 is renumbered Art. 224. Remember the chain: (a) inspect -> (f) require records -> Rule X details -> Art. 119 punishes lies.

provisions.citation: Omnibus Rules, Book III, Rule X, Sec. 11
provisions.verbatim: SECTION 11. Place of records. — All employment records of the employees shall be kept and maintained by the employer in or about the premises of the work place. The premises of a work-place shall be understood to mean the main or branch office of the establishment, if any, depending upon where the employees are regularly assigned. The keeping of the employee's records in another place is prohibited.
provisions.explanation: Syllabus prohibition #9 ('keeping of records in a place other than the workplace' — the syllabus gives no citation; this is it): employment records live IN OR ABOUT the workplace (main or branch office where the workers are regularly assigned) — keeping them elsewhere is PROHIBITED. The purpose is inspection-readiness under Art. 128(a): records must be where inspectors arrive. Context: Rule X Secs. 6-10 detail payroll contents, time-record methods (bundy clock/timekeeper/DTR forms), ink-and-chronological filing, and production records for non-time workers; Sec. 12 requires 3-year preservation. Remember: off-site-only records (e.g., sole copies at a distant head office) violate this section.

provisions.citation: Omnibus Rules, Book III, Rule X, Sec. 13
provisions.verbatim: SECTION 13. False reporting. — It shall be unlawful for any employer or any person to make any false statement, report or record on matters required to be kept or maintained pursuant to the provisions of this Rule.
provisions.explanation: The regulatory twin of Art. 119, completing the syllabus's '119; 128(f); Rule X, Sec. 13' citation chain: falsifying anything Rule X requires kept (payrolls, time records, production records) is unlawful. Art. 119 adds the 'knowing' and 'material' qualifiers at statute level. Compliance moral: the records the visitorial power can demand (Art. 128(a)/(f)) must be both PRESENT (Rule X Sec. 11) and TRUE (Art. 119 + this section). Remember Mabeza's lesson: self-serving summaries prepared after the fact, without payrolls and receipts, prove nothing.

provisions.citation: Civil Code, Art. 1708
provisions.verbatim: Art. 1708. The laborer's wages shall not be subject to execution or attachment, except for debts incurred for food, shelter, clothing and medical attendance.
provisions.explanation: Syllabus prohibition #10 (garnishment/execution): wages are generally EXEMPT from levy — the worker's lifeline cannot be seized for ordinary debts. Only FOUR necessities pierce the shield: food, shelter, clothing, and medical attendance. This is a Civil Code (not Labor Code) protection, and it binds creditors and sheriffs, not the employer. Remember the quartet: food-shelter-clothing-medicine — any other garnishment of wages is void as against this article.

provisions.citation: PD 851, Secs. 1-2 (13th-month pay)
provisions.verbatim:
SECTION 1. All employers are hereby required to pay all their employees receiving a basic salary of not more than P1,000 a month, regardless of the nature of their employment, a 13th-month pay not later than December 24 of every year. [Salary ceiling REMOVED by Memorandum Order No. 28 (1986) — current coverage is all rank-and-file employees regardless of salary; see prov.rev13th-guidelines.]

SEC. 2. Employers already paying their employees a 13th-month pay or its equivalent are not covered by this Decree.
provisions.explanation: The decree that created 13th-month pay (1975): a mandatory year-end benefit due by December 24. Sec. 1's P1,000 ceiling is DEAD — MO 28 (1986) lifted it, and the 1987 Revised Guidelines restate coverage as all rank-and-file employees with >=1 month of service, regardless of salary (managerial employees excluded). Sec. 2's 'already paying' exemption survives in revised form: Christmas bonus, mid-year bonus, profit-sharing, and other payments count ONLY to the extent they meet or exceed 1/12 of basic salary — any shortfall must be topped up, and Anniversary/CBA-signing bonuses and profit-sharing are cash-and-stock-dividend equivalents, not automatic credits (Revised Guidelines item 2(b)-(c)). Arco Metal's CBA-signing bonuses were tested exactly this way. Remember: PD 851 states the mandate; the Guidelines state the current mechanics; Boie-Takeda states the commissions rule.

provisions.citation: Revised Guidelines on the Implementation of the 13th Month Pay Law (1987), items 1, 2, 3(b), 5, 6
provisions.verbatim:
1. Coverage. The law covers all rank-and-file employees. For this purpose the term 'rank-and-file employee' shall mean an employee not falling under the definition of 'managerial employee'.

2. Exempted Employers. The following employers are still not covered: (a) The Government and any of its political subdivisions, including government-owned and controlled corporations, except those corporations operating essentially as private subsidiaries of the Government; (b) Employers who are already paying their employees 13th-month pay or more in a calendar year or its equivalent at the time of the issuance of the guidelines; (c) Employers of household helpers and persons in the personal service of another in relation to such workers; and (d) Employers of those who are paid on purely commission, boundary, or task basis, and those who are paid a fixed amount for performing specific work, irrespective of the time consumed in the performance thereof, except where the workers are paid on piece-rate basis in which case the employer shall grant them 13th-month pay not less than 1/12th of the total earnings each employee has received during the calendar year.

[...] 3. Nature of Payment. [...] (b) Minimum of the Amount. The minimum 13th-month pay shall not be less than 1/12 of the total basic salary earned by an employee within a calendar year. [...]

5. 13th-Month Pay for Certain Types of Employees. (a) Employees Paid on Piece-Rate Basis. [...] (b) Employees Paid by Results. Employees who are paid on piece-rate basis shall be entitled to the 13th-month pay. Employees with multiple employers. Government employees working part time in a private enterprise, including private educational institutions, as well as employees working in two or more private firms, whether on full or part time basis regardless of their salary with only one employer, shall be entitled to 13th month pay by all private employers. Private school teachers. Private school teachers, including faculty members of universities and colleges, are entitled to 13th month pay, regardless of the number of months they teach or are paid within a year, if they have rendered service for at least one (1) month within a year.

6. 13th-Month Pay of Resigned or Separated Employee. An employee who has resigned or whose services were terminated at any time before the time for payment of the 13th-month pay shall be entitled to this monetary benefit in proportion to the length of time he worked during the year, reckoned from the time he started working during the calendar year up to the time of his resignation or termination from the service. The payment of the 13th-month pay may be demanded by the employee upon the cessation of employer-employee relationship. This provision shall apply to any kind of separation from employment thus, it applies to employees who are dismissed, those who resigned and those who were separated by reason of... disability, death or other causes. The exception is where an employee is paid separation pay on account of his separation. Where the company grants separation pay equivalent to at least one month salary in addition to the 13th month pay earned during the year, no exemption can be claimed.
provisions.explanation: The current operating rules (with Boie-Takeda corrections noted). Coverage: rank-and-file ONLY (managerial excluded). Exemptions: government (which has its own year-end bonus regime), already-paying employers, household/personal-service employers, and purely-commission/boundary/task workers — BUT piece-rate workers ARE covered at 1/12 of total earnings (David's butcher lost on the task-basis exemption, a piece-rate worker would win). Amount: minimum 1/12 of total BASIC salary (excludes OT, premium, NSD, holiday pay, COLA, unused-leave cash — unless integrated by agreement/practice). Multiple employers: collect from ALL private employers. Resigned/separated (any cause incl. death/disability/dismissal): PROPORTIONATE 13th month, demandable upon separation — and separation pay of >=1 month does NOT cancel it. Payment deadline: December 24 (may split 1/2 before school opening + 1/2 by Dec 24). Remember Boie-Takeda's voiding: item 5(a)'s 2nd paragraph (fixed wage + commission on total earnings) is VOID — commissions never enter 13th-month basic salary.

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 95 (renumbered; same number as original)
provisions.verbatim:
ART. 95. Right to Service Incentive Leave. (a) Every employee who has rendered at least one year of service shall be entitled to a yearly service incentive leave of five days with pay.

(b) This provision shall not apply to those who are already enjoying the benefit herein provided, those enjoying vacation leave with pay of at least five days and those employed in establishments regularly employing less than ten employees or in establishments exempted from granting this benefit by the Secretary of Labor and Employment after considering the viability or financial condition of such establishment.

(c) The grant of benefit in excess of that provided herein shall not be made a subject for arbitration or any court or administrative action.
provisions.explanation: The statutory 5-day paid leave: every employee with >=1 year of service gets 5 days with pay yearly (Rule V: 'one year' = 12 months from hiring, whether or not continuous within the calendar year; unused SIL is COMMUTABLE to cash at year-end). Three non-applicabilities: (1) already enjoying this benefit, (2) already enjoying >=5 days vacation leave with pay (no stacking on equivalent-or-better vacation), (3) <10-employee establishments or Secretary-exempted (viability/financial condition). Paragraph (c): generosity beyond 5 days is purely voluntary — it cannot be compelled by arbitration or suit (but voluntarily granted excess CAN ripen into practice under Art. 100 — Arco Metal logic). David + Auto Bus: pakyaw/task AND commission workers get SIL unless they are field personnel. Remember: SIL is the FLOOR (5 days); vacation leave >=5 days satisfies it; unused days convert to cash.

provisions.citation: Omnibus Rules, Book III, Rule V, Secs. 1-3, 5
provisions.verbatim:
SECTION 1. Coverage. — This rule shall apply to all employees except: (a) Those of the government and any of the political subdivisions, including government-owned and controlled corporations; (b) Domestic helpers and persons in the personal service of another; (c) Managerial employees as defined in Book Three of the Code; (d) Field personnel and other employees whose performance is unsupervised by the employer including those who are engaged on task or contract basis, purely commission basis, or those who are paid a fixed amount for performing work irrespective of the time consumed in the performance thereof; (e) Those who are already enjoying the benefit herein provided; (f) Those enjoying vacation leave with pay of at least five days; and (g) Those employed in establishments regularly employing less than ten employees.

SECTION 2. Right to service incentive leave. — Every employee who has rendered at least one year of service shall be entitled to a yearly service incentive leave of five (5) days with pay.

SECTION 3. Definition of one year of service. — The term 'at least one year of service' shall mean service within 12 months, whether continuous or broken, reckoned from the date the employee started working, including authorized absences and paid regular holidays unless the working days in the establishment as a matter of practice or policy, or that provided in the employment contracts, is less than 12 months, in which case said period shall be considered as one year.

[...] SECTION 5. Commutation of service incentive leave. — The service incentive leave shall be commutable to its money equivalent at the end of the year: Provided, That the employer shall pay his employees including those who have resigned, were terminated or separated from the employment on account of closure of the enterprise or reduction in force any unused service incentive leave or any portion thereof equivalent to the ratio which the length of service of the employee during the year bears to the entire year: Provided, That such leave may be used for sick and other leave purposes which are not paid under existing laws, collective bargaining agreement, or company policy.
provisions.explanation: Rule V operationalizes Art. 95. Sec. 3's one-year rule is generous: 12 months from hiring, CONTINUOUS OR BROKEN, counting authorized absences and paid holidays (short-season establishments' working period counts as a year). Sec. 5 commutation: unused SIL converts to CASH at year-end — INCLUDING resigned/terminated/separated employees, prorated by months served (Auto Bus commuted 3 years of SIL on separation). The last sentence lets SIL double as sick/emergency leave where no paid equivalent exists. Sec. 1(d)'s task/commission phrase is read WITH 'field personnel' (David, Auto Bus, ejusdem generis) — supervised non-time workers are COVERED. Remember: SIL accrues after the first 12 months and unused days NEVER expire uncompensated — they commute.

provisions.citation: RA 11861, Secs. 3-4 (amending RA 8972 Secs. 3-4; solo-parent definitions and categories)
provisions.verbatim:
"Section 3. Definition of Terms. — [...] (b) Children refer to those living with and dependent upon the solo parent for support who are unmarried, unemployed and not more than twenty-two (22) years of age, or even over (22) years old but are unable to fully take care or protect themselves from abuse, neglect, cruelty, exploitation, or discrimination because of a physical or mental disability or condition: Provided, That this definition shall only apply for the purpose of this Act: Provided, further, That a person below twenty-two (22) years old who gives birth as a result of rape or other crimes against chastity as defined under Title Eleven, Act No. 3815, as amended, the Revised Penal Code, even without losing parental authority, shall also be considered a solo parent under this Act: [...]"

"Sec. 4. Categories of Solo Parent.- A solo parent refers to any individual who falls under any of the following categories: (1) A parent who provides sole parental care and support of the child or children due to - (a) Birth as a consequence of rape, even without final conviction [...] (b) Death of the spouse; (c) Detention of the spouse for at least three (3) months or service of sentence for a criminal conviction; (d) Physical or mental incapacity of the spouse as certified by a public or private medical practitioner; (e) Legal separation or de facto separation for at least six (6) months, and the solo parent is entrusted with the sole parental care and support of the child or children; (f) Declaration of nullity or annulment of marriage, as decreed by a court or by the church, or divorce, as may be applicable, and the solo parent is entrusted with the sole parental care and support of the child or children; or (g) Abandonment or disappearance of the spouse for at least six (6) months; (2) A spouse or any family member of an OFW, or the guardian of the child or children of an OFW [...]; (3) An unmarried mother or father who keeps and rears the child or children; (4) A legal guardian, adoptive or foster parent who solely provides parental care and support; (5) A relative within the fourth (4th) civil degree of consanguinity or affinity of the parent or legal guardian who assumes parental care and support [...] as a result of death, abandonment, disappearance or absence of the parents or solo parent [...] for at least six (6) months [...]; (6) A pregnant woman who provides sole parental care and support to the unborn child or children; and (7) Any other person who solely provides parental care and support to a child or children: Provided, That the child or children [...] are living with and dependent upon the solo parent for support." [...] A change in the status or circumstance of the solo parent claiming benefits under this Act, such that the solo parent is no longer eligible, shall terminate eligibility. [...]
provisions.explanation: The CURRENT solo-parent definition (replacing RA 8972 Sec. 3(a)). Two parts: CHILDREN (unmarried, unemployed, <=22, living with and dependent on the solo parent; over-22s with disability included) and the SEVEN solo-parent categories — rape-consequence birth, spousal death, detention/sentence, incapacity, separation (legal/de facto >=6 months), nullity/annulment/divorce, abandonment/disappearance (>=6 months) under (1); OFW-family/guardian (2); unmarried parent (3); guardian/adoptive/foster (4); up-to-4th-degree relative stepping in (5); solo pregnant woman (6); and the (7) catch-all. Status change ends eligibility. Exam use: this provision answers 'who qualifies' before Sec. 8's leave mechanics. Remember: the RA 8972 'Sec. 20' syllabus citation is erroneous (that law has only Secs. 1-17) — the operative law is RA 11861 throughout.

provisions.citation: RA 8972, Sec. 8, as amended by RA 11861, Sec. 7 (solo-parent parental leave)
provisions.verbatim: "Sec. 8. Parental Leave. - Notwithstanding exiting [sic] laws, rules and regulations to the contrary, a forfeitable and noncumulative parental leave of not more than seven (7) working days with pay every year shall be granted to any solo parent employee, regardless of employment status, who has rendered service of at least six (6) months. [...] Provided, That the parental leave under this Section may be availed of to fulfil parental obligations such as attending to the needs of the child or children despite other existing wellness or health programs of the employer: Provided, further, That the employer, whether in the public or private sector, shall not discriminate against an employee availing of parental leave by withholding from any employee availing of parental leave under this Act any company policy-related bonuses by reason of the availment of parental leave under this Act: [...]"
provisions.explanation: The current parental-leave rule: 7 WORKING days with pay yearly, FORFEITABLE and NONCUMULATIVE (use-it-or-lose-it — no carryover, unlike SIL's commutation), available after only 6 MONTHS of service (halved from RA 8972's 1 year), to ANY solo-parent employee in public OR private sector regardless of employment status. Usable for parental obligations (child's needs) even alongside company wellness programs; anti-discrimination proviso bars withholding policy bonuses BECAUSE of leave availment. Contrast with SIL: SIL commutes to cash, parental leave forfeits; SIL needs 12 months, parental needs 6. Remember the pair: 7 days / 6 months / forfeitable — the mirror image of SIL's 5 days / 12 months / commutable.

provisions.citation: RA 11210, Secs. 3-6 (105-day maternity leave)
provisions.verbatim:
SEC. 3. Grant of Maternity Leave. - All covered female workers in government and the private sector, including those in the informal economy, regardless of civil status or the legitimacy of her child, shall be granted one hundred five (105) days maternity leave with full pay and an option to extend for an additional thirty (30) days without pay: Provided, That in case the worker qualifies as a solo parent under Republic Act No. 8972, or the 'Solo Parents' Welfare Act of 2000,' the worker shall be granted an additional fifteen (15) days maternity leave with full pay.

Enjoyment of maternity leave cannot be deferred but should be availed of either before or after the actual period of delivery in a continuous and uninterrupted manner, as follows: (1) Sixty (60) days before delivery, except in case of miscarriage or emergency termination of pregnancy; (2) Sixty (60) days after delivery, except in case of miscarriage or emergency termination of pregnancy where the entitled maternity leave benefit shall be sixty (60) days.

SEC. 4. Maternity Leave for Female Workers in the Public Sector. - Any pregnant female worker in the government service, regardless of employment status, agency or instrumentality, and including those in government-owned or -controlled corporations, shall be granted a maternity leave of one hundred five (105) days with full pay regardless of whether she gave birth through caesarian section or natural delivery, while maternity leave of sixty (60) days with full pay shall be granted for miscarriage or emergency termination of pregnancy.

SEC. 5. Maternity Leave for Female Workers in the Private Sector. - Any pregnant female worker in the private sector shall be granted a maternity leave of one hundred five (105) days with full pay, regardless of whether she gave birth through caesarian [sic] section or natural delivery, while maternity leave of sixty (60) days with full pay shall be granted for miscarriage or emergency termination of pregnancy: Provided, That to be entitled to the maternity leave benefits, a female worker should be an SSS member who has paid at least three (3) monthly contributions in the twelve (12)-month period immediately preceding the semester of her childbirth, miscarriage, or emergency termination of pregnancy: Provided, further, That the maternity benefit shall be paid by the SSS directly to the female worker: Provided, finally, That the female worker should notify the SSS through her employer of her pregnancy and the probable date of her childbirth, among others.

Full payment of the maternity leave benefit shall be advanced by the employer within thirty (30) days from the filing of the maternity leave application. Thereafter, post-payment of the SSS grant or a reimbursement from SSS shall be made to the employer immediately upon receipt of satisfactory and legal proof of such payment for the maternity leave: Provided, That the SSS shall immediately reimburse the employer of one hundred percent (100%) of the amount of maternity benefits advanced to the female worker by the employer upon receipt of satisfactory and legal proof of such payment.

The maternity leave credits and benefits provided under this Act shall be granted to Kasambahays and female workers in the informal economy.

Women workers in the private sector covered by Republic Act No. 8282, otherwise known as the 'Social Security Act of 1997,' shall receive benefits equivalent to one hundred percent (100%) of their average daily salary credit for sixty (60) days in case of miscarriage or emergency termination of pregnancy, and one hundred (100) days in case of live childbirth, regardless of the mode of delivery, and an additional fifteen (15) days paid maternity leave shall also be granted to solo parents as defined under Republic Act No. 8972. An additional maternity leave of thirty (30) days, without pay, can be availed of, at the option of the female worker, without violating the security of tenure principle.

Maternity leave benefits granted under this Act shall be in lieu of any other similar maternity benefits that may be granted to pregnant female workers: Provided, That where other laws or collective bargaining agreements or employment contracts provide for maternity leave benefits more than those provided for under this Act, the female worker shall be entitled to such benefits.

Female workers availing of the maternity leave period and benefits must receive not less than two-thirds (2/3) of their regular monthly wages. For this purpose, employers from the private sector with female workers, who are voluntary SSS members while pregnant, shall remit all SSS contributions payments to the SSS in favor of the female workers and provide them their salary differentials.

The following are exempted from providing the salary differential requirements of this section: (1) Distressed establishments; (2) Retail/service establishments and other enterprises employing not more than ten (10) employees; (3) Microbusiness enterprises with total assets of not more than Three million pesos (P3,000,000.00); and (4) Enterprises already providing similar benefits, including benefits granted through collective bargaining agreements.

SEC. 6. Allocation of Maternity Leave Credits. - Any female worker entitled to maternity leave benefits as provided for herein may, at her option, allocate up to seven (7) days of said benefits to the child's father, whether or not the same is married to the female worker: Provided, That in the case of the death, absence, or incapacity of the father, the benefit may be allocated to an alternate caregiver who shall be either the current partner, whether or not the same is of the same sex as the female worker, or any of the grandparents, parents, siblings, and other relatives or qualified domestic caregivers: Provided, That written notice to the employers shall be given by the female worker and the alternate caregiver as well as the SSS: Provided, further, That this benefit shall be over and above that which is provided under Republic Act No. 8187, otherwise known as the 'Paternity Leave Act of 1996'. In the event the father or the alternate caregiver dies or becomes incapacitated, either before the 7-day leave or while on leave, said leave shall revert to the female worker.
provisions.explanation: The flagship leave law. Sec. 3: 105 DAYS with full pay per pregnancy (every pregnancy now — the old 4-pregnancy cap is gone), +30 optional unpaid, +15 for solo parents; miscarriage/emergency termination = 60 days. Secs. 4-5: public AND private (incl. kasambahays, informal economy) covered regardless of civil status/legitimacy/delivery mode. Private-sector mechanics: SSS member + 3 contributions in the 12 months before the semester of childbirth; employer ADVANCES full pay within 30 days of application, SSS reimburses 100%; employer pays the SALARY DIFFERENTIAL (full pay minus SSS grant) unless exempt (distressed, retail/service <=10, micro <=P3M assets, already-providing). Floor: at least 2/3 of regular monthly wages. Sec. 6: up to 7 days ALLOCABLE to the father (married or not) or, on his death/absence/incapacity, an alternate caregiver — OVER AND ABOVE RA 8187 paternity leave; reverts to the mother if the recipient dies/is incapacitated. Remember the 105/60/30/15/7 ladder and that benefits are 'in lieu of' lesser ones but yield to BETTER CBA/contract benefits.

provisions.citation: RA 8187, Secs. 2-3 (paternity leave grant and definition)
provisions.verbatim:
SECTION 2. Every married male employee in the private and public sectors shall be entitled to a paternity leave of seven (7) days with full pay for first four (4) deliveries of the legitimate spouse with whom he is cohabiting. The male employee shall apply for paternity leave by notifying his employer of his wife's pregnancy and his intention to avail of the benefits under this Act. Such application shall be supported by the physician's certification that the wife has indeed given birth or suffered a miscarriage; Provided, That delivery shall include childbirth, miscarriage, or abortion. Entitlement to paternity leave benefits under this Act for subsequent deliveries after the first four (4) shall be in accordance with the rules and regulations that the Secretary of Labor and Employment shall prescribe.

SECTION 3. For purposes of this Act, paternity leave shall mean the benefits granted to a married male employee allowing him to not report for work for seven (7) days but continues to earn the compensation therefor, on the condition that his spouse has delivered a child or suffered a miscarriage for purposes of enabling him to effectively lend support to his wife in her period of recovery and/or in the nursing of the newly-born child.
provisions.explanation: 7 days with full pay to MARRIED male employees (private + public) for the FIRST FOUR deliveries of the cohabiting legitimate spouse — delivery INCLUDES miscarriage/abortion, and entitlement needs notice + physician's certification. The syllabus cites Sec. 3 (the definition: paid non-reporting to support the wife's recovery and nurse the newborn); Sec. 2 supplies the grant and its limits. Two distinctions examiners test: (1) legitimacy/cohabitation conditions here vs. RA 11210 Sec. 6's allocation (no marriage requirement, over and above this Act); (2) the 4-delivery cap vs. maternity's every-pregnancy rule. Remember: paternity = married, 4 deliveries, 7 days; maternity allocation = any father/partner/relative, over and above.

provisions.citation: RA 9710, Sec. 18 (special leave benefits for women)
provisions.verbatim: SEC. 18. Special Leave Benefits for Women. - A woman employee having rendered continuous aggregate employment service of at least six (6) months for the last twelve (12) months shall be entitled to a special leave benefit of two (2) months with full pay based on her gross monthly compensation following surgery caused by gynecological disorders.
provisions.explanation: The 'gynecological leave': 2 MONTHS with full pay (based on GROSS monthly compensation) after surgery caused by gynecological disorders, requiring 6 months aggregate service in the last 12 months. Three limiters: (1) only female employees; (2) only SURGERY-caused (consultation/medication alone does not trigger it); (3) only gynecological disorders. Compare: maternity (RA 11210) pays via SSS + differential and needs no 6-month rule; this benefit is employer-paid at full gross pay. Remember: 2 months / surgery / gynecological / 6-in-12.

provisions.citation: RA 9262, Sec. 3(c) and Sec. 43 (battered woman syndrome; VAWC leave)
provisions.verbatim:
SECTION 3. Definition of Terms. — As used in this Act: [...] (c) 'Battered Woman Syndrome' refers to a scientifically defined pattern of psychological and behavioral symptoms found in women living in battering relationships as a result of cumulative abuse;

SECTION 43. Entitlement to Leave. — Victims under this Act shall be entitled to take a paid leave of absence up to ten (10) days in addition to other paid leaves under the Labor Code and Civil Service Rules and Regulations, extendible when the necessity arises as specified in the protection order. Any employer who shall prejudice the right of the person under this section shall be penalized in accordance with the provisions of the Labor Code and Civil Service Rules and Regulations. Likewise, an employer who shall prejudice any person for assisting a co-employee who is a victim under this Act shall likewise be liable for discrimination.
provisions.explanation: The VAWC leave: victims get up to 10 DAYS paid leave IN ADDITION to all other paid leaves (SIL, parental, etc. — it stacks, never substitutes), extendible per the protection order. BWS (Sec. 3(c)) is the defined psychological pattern of cumulative abuse — the provision's conceptual anchor and a justifying circumstance in the penal context (outside this module). Two employer duties: (1) grant the leave (prejudice is penalized under labor/CSC rules); (2) never prejudice co-employees who ASSIST a victim (liable for discrimination). Remember: 10 days / stacks on top / extendible via protection order / assistance-protection included.

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 58 (renumbered; same number as original)
provisions.verbatim: ART. 58. Definition of Terms. As used in this Title: (a) "Apprenticeship" means practical training on the job supplemented by related theoretical instruction. (b) An "apprentice" is a worker who is covered by a written apprenticeship agreement with an individual employer or any of the entities recognized under this Chapter. (c) An "apprenticeable occupation" means any trade, form of employment or occupation which requires more than three (3) months of practical training on the job supplemented by related theoretical instruction. (d) "Apprenticeship agreement" is an employment contract wherein the employer binds himself to train the apprentice and the apprentice in turn accepts the terms of training.
provisions.explanation: Four interlocking definitions. Apprenticeship = OJT PLUS related theoretical instruction (pure OJT without theory is not apprenticeship); an apprentice exists only under a WRITTEN apprenticeship agreement (no writing, no apprentice status — the worker defaults to regular employment analysis); an apprenticeable occupation needs MORE THAN 3 months of training (the 3-month line also separates apprentices from learners); and the agreement is itself an EMPLOYMENT contract (train-me / I-accept-training), so apprentices are employees with full labor-standards coverage except as the chapter provides. Practical application: TESDA/DOLE-approved programs and the written agreement are the employer's only proof of apprentice status in a regularization dispute. Remember: written + >3 months + theory = apprentice.

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 59 (renumbered; same number as original)
provisions.verbatim:
ART. 59. Qualifications of Apprentice. To qualify as an apprentice, a person shall: (a) Be at least fourteen (14) years of age; (b) Possess vocational aptitude and capacity for appropriate tests; and (c) Possess the ability to comprehend and follow oral and written instructions.

Trade, industry and labor organizations may recommend to the Secretary of Labor and Employment appropriate educational requirements for different occupations.
provisions.explanation: Three qualifications: age 14+, vocational aptitude (testable), and ability to follow oral/written instructions. Currency note: the 14-year floor predates RA 9231 (2003), which now generally bars employment below 15 outside narrow family/non-hazardous exceptions — teach RA 9231 as the operative child-labor floor and Art. 59(a) as the chapter's internal rule (outside the syllabus citation, noted for accuracy). Industry/labor groups may recommend educational requirements through the Secretary. Remember: aptitude + comprehension are substantive — apprenticeship is training for the trainable, not cheap labor by another name.

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 60 (renumbered; same number as original)
provisions.verbatim: ART. 60. Employment of Apprentices. Only employers in the highly technical industries may employ apprentices and only in apprenticeable occupations approved by the Secretary of Labor and Employment.
provisions.explanation: The double gate on apprentice hiring: (1) the EMPLOYER must be in a highly technical industry, and (2) the OCCUPATION must be a Secretary-approved apprenticeable one. A retail shop or restaurant cannot 'hire apprentices' — the status is reserved for technical trades needing extended structured training. Enforcement consequence: workers hired as 'apprentices' outside these gates are analyzed as regular employees from day one. Remember: highly-technical-industry employer + approved occupation — fail either and the apprentice label collapses.

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 61 (renumbered; same number as original)
provisions.verbatim: ART. 61. Contents of Apprenticeship Agreements. Apprenticeship agreements, including the wage rates of apprentices, shall conform to the rules issued by the Secretary of Labor and Employment. The period of apprenticeship shall not exceed six (6) months. Apprenticeship agreements providing for wage rates below the legal minimum wage, which in no case shall start below 75 per cent of the applicable minimum wage, may be entered into only in accordance with apprenticeship programs duly approved by the Secretary of Labor and Employment. The Ministry shall develop standard model programs of apprenticeship.
provisions.explanation: Three controls: (1) the agreement must conform to Secretary rules (including wage rates); (2) the period CANNOT exceed 6 MONTHS — work beyond 6 months under the same arrangement converts toward regular employment; (3) sub-minimum apprentice wages are allowed ONLY within approved programs and NEVER below 75% of the applicable minimum wage — this is the syllabus's '61' under minimum wage. Compare: learners 75% (Art. 75(c)), PWDs 75% (Art. 80 par. 2), and Art. 124's auto-modification of training wage clauses on every wage increase. Practical application: calendar the 6-month expiry and re-verify the 75%-of-current-minimum floor after each wage order. Remember: 6 months max / 75% min / approved program only.

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 72 (renumbered; same number as original)
provisions.verbatim: ART. 72. Apprentices Without Compensation. The Secretary of Labor and Employment may authorize the hiring of apprentices without compensation whose training on the job is required by the school, training institution or curriculum, as approved by the appropriate government authority.
provisions.explanation: The ONLY unpaid apprenticeship: school/curriculum-required OJT, individually AUTHORIZED by the Secretary. Two cumulative conditions — (1) the training is required by the school/institution/curriculum as approved by government authority, AND (2) the Secretary authorizes the specific hiring. Without both, the 75% floor (Art. 61) applies. This is the practicum/OJT provision: it covers students earning academic credit, not 'trainees' doing productive work for free. Remember: unpaid requires school-requirement PLUS Secretary authorization — employer say-so alone never suffices.

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 73 (renumbered; same number as original)
provisions.verbatim: ART. 73. Definition of Learners. Learners are persons hired as trainees in semi-skilled and other industrial occupations which are non-apprenticeable and which may be learned through practical training on the job in a relatively short period of time which shall not exceed three (3) months.
provisions.explanation: The learner in one sentence: trainee + semi-skilled/non-apprenticeable occupation + OJT-learnable in <=3 MONTHS. The 3-month ceiling is the bright line against apprentices (>3 months + theory): learnership is for jobs learnable fast. 'Non-apprenticeable' means the occupation cannot qualify under Art. 58(c) — the two chapters are mutually exclusive by design. Remember: semi-skilled + non-apprenticeable + 3 months max = learner.

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 74 (renumbered; same number as original)
provisions.verbatim: ART. 74. When Learners May Be Hired. Learners may be employed when no experienced workers are available, the employment of learners is necessary to prevent curtailment of employment opportunities, and the employment does not create unfair competition in terms of labor costs or impair or lower working standards.
provisions.explanation: Three cumulative justifications for hiring learners: (1) no experienced workers AVAILABLE (a labor-market condition, not a preference); (2) NECESSARY to prevent curtailment of employment opportunities (training keeps jobs open); (3) no UNFAIR labor-cost competition and no impairment of working standards (learners cannot undercut regulars' wages/conditions). This is the anti-abuse gate: an employer fully staffed with experienced regulars cannot rotate 'learners' to save 25% on wages. Remember: unavailability + necessity + no-undercutting — all three, every time.

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 75 (renumbered; same number as original)
provisions.verbatim: ART. 75. Learnership Agreement. Any employer desiring to employ learners shall enter into a learnership agreement with them, which agreement shall include: (a) The names and addresses of the learners; (b) The duration of the learnership period, which shall not exceed three (3) months; (c) The wages or salary rates of the learners which shall begin at not less than seventy-five percent (75%) of the applicable minimum wages; and (d) A commitment to employ the learners if they so desire, as regular employees upon completion of the learnership. All learners who have been allowed or suffered to work during the first two (2) months shall be deemed regular employees if training is terminated by the employer before the end of the stipulated period through no fault of the learners.
provisions.explanation: The learnership agreement's four mandatory contents: names/addresses, duration (<=3 months), wage (>=75% of minimum — the syllabus's '75(c)' under minimum wage), and the COMMITMENT to hire as regulars on completion if they so desire. The sting is in the tail: learners allowed/suffered to work the first 2 months become REGULAR employees if the employer cuts training short through no fault of theirs — early termination converts status automatically. Compare apprentices: no parallel auto-regularization sentence exists in Arts. 58-61 (regularization follows general Art. 281/295 principles instead). Practical application: never terminate a learnership before month 3 without documented learner fault. Remember: 75% floor + hire-commitment + 2-month conversion tripwire.

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 76 (renumbered; same number as original)
provisions.verbatim: ART. 76. Learners in Piecework. Learners employed in piece or incremental work shall be paid in full for the work done.
provisions.explanation: One line with real bite: piece-rate learners get NO training discount — they are paid IN FULL for output. The 75% floor of Art. 75(c) governs time-rated learnership; once pay is per piece, the learner earns the full piece rate from day one. Rationale: piece rates already self-adjust for inexperience (slower hands earn less). Remember: time-learners 75%, piece-learners 100%.

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 78 (renumbered; same number as original)
provisions.verbatim: ART. 78. Definition. Handicapped workers are those whose earning capacity is impaired by age or physical or mental deficiency or injury.
provisions.explanation: The chapter's gateway definition: earning capacity IMPAIRED by age, physical/mental deficiency, or injury. Terminology note: the Code says 'handicapped workers'; current usage (RA 7277 onward) is persons with disabilities (PWDs) — the syllabus itself uses 'PWDs (78-81)'. The definition's pivot is IMPAIRED EARNING CAPACITY, not the disability label alone — which is why Art. 79 tests employability against the specific work. Remember: impairment + earning-capacity effect = chapter coverage.

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 79 (renumbered; same number as original)
provisions.verbatim: ART. 79. When Employable. Handicapped workers may be employed when their employment is necessary to prevent curtailment of employment opportunities and when it does not create unfair competition in labor costs or impair or lower working standards.
provisions.explanation: The PWD twin of Art. 74's learner gate: employment must be NECESSARY to prevent curtailment of opportunities AND must not undercut labor costs or working standards. Same anti-abuse logic — the sub-minimum wage permission (Art. 80 par. 2) exists to OPEN jobs, never to cheapen them. Note the deliberate omission versus Art. 74: no 'no experienced workers available' condition — PWD hiring is encouraged even where experienced workers exist. Remember: necessity + no-undercutting (no unavailability requirement).

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 80 (renumbered; same number as original)
provisions.verbatim:
ART. 80. Employment Agreement.
