Any employer who employs handicapped workers shall enter into an employment agreement with them, which agreement shall include: (a) The names and addresses of the handicapped workers to be employed; (b) The rate to be paid the handicapped workers which shall not be less than seventy five (75%) percent of the applicable legal minimum wage; (c) The duration of employment period; and (d) The work to be performed by handicapped workers.

The employment agreement shall be subject to inspection by the Secretary of Labor and Employment or his duly authorized representatives.
provisions.explanation: Four mandatory contents mirroring learnership: names, rate (>=75% of legal minimum — the syllabus's '80 par. 2' under minimum wage), duration, and the work to be performed. The inspection sentence makes the agreement a DOLE-auditable document (cf. Art. 128(a)). Pair with Art. 81: PWDs meeting apprentice/learner qualifications train under THOSE chapters' rules — Art. 80 governs PWDs hired as workers, not trainees. Practical application: keep the written agreement on file at the workplace (Rule X Sec. 11 logic) with the 75% floor recomputed per current wage order. Remember: same four corners as learnership, but for employment rather than training.

provisions.citation: Labor Code, Art. 81 (renumbered; same number as original)
provisions.verbatim: ART. 81. Eligibility for Apprenticeship. Subject to the appropriate provisions of this Code, handicapped workers may be hired as apprentices or learners if their handicap is not such as to effectively impede the performance of job operations in the particular occupations for which they are hired.
provisions.explanation: The bridge article: PWDs may train as APPRENTICES or LEARNERS whenever the handicap does not effectively impede the particular job's operations — channeling them into Arts. 58-72 (with theory, >3 months, 6-month cap) or Arts. 73-76 (semi-skilled, <=3 months, hire-commitment) as the occupation fits. The test is job-specific ('in the particular occupations'), not categorical: a mobility impairment barring warehouse apprenticeship is irrelevant to a desk-based learnership. RA 7277 Sec. 7 restates the same eligibility for the modern regime. Remember: Art. 81 routes PWD TRAINEES to the apprentice/learner chapters; Arts. 78-80 govern PWD WORKERS.

provisions.citation: RA 7277, Sec. 5 (equal opportunity for employment)
provisions.verbatim: SECTION 5. Equal Opportunity for Employment. — No disabled persons shall be denied access to opportunities for suitable employment. A qualified disabled employee shall be subject to the same terms and conditions of employment and the same compensation, privileges, benefits, fringe benefits, incentives or allowances as a qualified able-bodied person.
provisions.explanation: The modern PWD employment rule sitting alongside Arts. 78-81: no denial of SUITABLE employment, and — once qualified — IDENTICAL terms, compensation, and benefits as able-bodied counterparts. The apparent tension with Art. 80's 75% floor resolves by scope: Art. 80's training-period rate applies during the covered employment-agreement period; Sec. 5 governs qualified PWD employees generally (equal pay for equal work — cf. Art. 133(a)'s 'work of equal value' logic). RA 7277 Sec. 6 reserves 5% of casual/emergency/contractual posts in listed social-development agencies for PWDs; Sec. 7 confirms apprenticeship eligibility. Later amendments (RA 9442, RA 10754) touched only privileges/discounts — this section stands as enacted. Remember: suitable-employment access + qualified-employee equality.

cases.citation: G.R. No. 159577, 3 May 2006, First Division (Panganiban, C.J.)
cases.facts: Petitioner, hired as a shift engineer/foreman at respondent's plywood plant (1975-1999), claimed overtime pay plus premium pay for rest days and special holidays. The company countered he was a managerial employee: he supervised the boiler section, oversaw 19-36 workers, and recommended personnel actions on approved forms.
cases.issue: Was petitioner a managerial employee exempt from Title I (hours of work) labor standards, and hence unentitled to overtime and premium pay?
cases.ruling: No as a MANAGERIAL EMPLOYEE, yes as exempt. The Court held petitioner did not meet all three Rule I Sec. 2(b) tests (he was never an employer/department manager whose primary duty was management; he reported to the plant manager). But he squarely met the Rule I Sec. 2(c) MANAGERIAL STAFF test (management-related work, discretion and independent judgment, supervision of shifts/sections, within the 20% cap). Either exemption removes the worker from Title I coverage — petition denied, no OT or premium pay due, though SIL pay stood unappealed.
cases.doctrine: Exemption from Title I labor standards turns on actual duties under Rule I Sec. 2, not job titles: failure of the managerial-employee test (Sec. 2(b)) does not save the claim if the worker qualifies as a member of the managerial staff (Sec. 2(c)).
cases.name: Penaranda v. Baganga Plywood Corp.

cases.citation: G.R. No. 195466, 2 July 2014, Second Division (Brion, J.)
cases.facts: Petitioner worked as a butcher (slaughterer) paid P40-50 per pig on pakyaw (task) basis. He filed money claims for holiday pay, SIL pay, and 13th-month pay; the employer denied an employment relationship, invoking the 'no employer-employee relationship for pakyaw workers' line.
cases.issue: Is a pakyaw (task-basis) worker an employee entitled to holiday pay, service incentive leave pay, and 13th-month pay?
cases.ruling: Yes to employment, holiday pay, and SIL — no to 13th-month pay. Pakyaw is a mode of payment (Art. 97/101), not proof of independence; control (supervision, fixed rules, regular reporting at the workplace) established employment under the four-fold test. Rules I, IV, V task-basis phrases are read with 'field personnel' (ejusdem generis; Serrano, Auto Bus, Cebu Institute) — petitioner's on-premises work with determinable hours was not field personnel, so holiday and SIL pay were due (burden of proof on the employer, unmet). 13th-month pay was denied: PD 851 Sec. 3(e) exempts task-basis workers WITHOUT a field-personnel qualifier. No 'independent contractor' finding was made.
cases.doctrine: (1) Pakyaw/task pay neither negates employment nor, without field-personnel status, defeats holiday and SIL pay — task-basis phrases in the Rules are construed with 'field personnel' by ejusdem generis; (2) the PD 851 task-basis exemption from 13th-month pay is absolute and admits no field-personnel qualification.
cases.name: David v. Macasio

cases.citation: G.R. No. 156367, 16 May 2005, Second Division (Chico-Nazario, J.)
cases.facts: Respondent, a driver-conductor paid 7% commission of gross bus revenue per trip (plus a fixed amount per bus, with some guaranteed allowance), claimed SIL pay for 3 years after separation. The company argued commission-basis drivers are not entitled to SIL.
cases.issue: Is a commission-basis driver-conductor 'field personnel' (or otherwise excluded) and hence unentitled to service incentive leave pay?
cases.ruling: No — SIL pay due. The driver was not field personnel: inspectors, dispatchers, depot assignments, and prescribed schedules proved supervision, with determinable hours (BWC advisory opinion quoted). Rule V Sec. 1(d)'s 'task or contract basis, purely commission basis' phrase is read with 'field personnel' (ejusdem generis); a supervised commission worker is covered. Three years of SIL were commuted to cash. (The Court also stated the SIL prescription rule — Art. 291 runs from demand/refusal — and left intact the deletion of the 13th-month award for purely-commission work.)
cases.doctrine: (1) Non-field-personnel status — supervision plus determinable hours — keeps commission-basis workers inside SIL coverage; task/commission phrases in Rule V Sec. 1(d) are construed with 'field personnel' (ejusdem generis); (2) SIL non-use commutes to cash, including on separation.
cases.name: Auto Bus Transport Systems, Inc. v. Bautista

cases.citation: G.R. Nos. 92174 and 102552, 10 December 1993, Second Division (Narvasa, C.J.)
cases.facts: Routine DOLE inspections of Boie-Takeda (medical representatives on fixed salary + commission) and Fuji Xerox (salesmen on fixed salary + commission) yielded deficiency findings for excluding commissions from 13th-month pay, affirmed by the Secretary under Revised Guidelines item 5(a) (fixed wage + commission computed on total earnings). Both employers went to the Supreme Court.
cases.issue: Are commissions part of 'basic salary' for 13th-month pay computation, and is Revised Guidelines item 5(a)'s second paragraph valid?
cases.ruling: No and void. Commissions are excluded from 13th-month 'basic salary': PD 851 and its 1975 Rules define basic salary to exclude earnings not integrated as part of the regular/basic salary, and the Guidelines themselves exclude 'earnings and other monetary benefits which are not part of or integrated into the regular salary.' The Court distinguished Songco (commissions are 'salary' GENERICALLY for separation-pay purposes) from 'basic salary' here, and declared item 5(a)'s second paragraph VOID for unduly expanding PD 851 beyond its letter and spirit. Inspection deficiencies were set aside.
cases.doctrine: Commissions, though 'salary' in the generic Art. 97(f)/Songco sense, are NOT part of 'basic salary' for 13th-month pay; an implementing rule that folds them into the 13th-month base is void for exceeding the decree.
cases.name: Boie-Takeda Chemicals, Inc. v. Dela Serna (with Phil. Fuji Xerox v. Dela Serna)

cases.citation: G.R. No. 170734, 14 May 2008, Second Division (Tinga, J.)
cases.facts: Seven company employees with under 12 months of service received full 13th-month pay, CBA-signing bonuses, service awards, and 1993-94 leave encashment identical to full-year employees (1992-2003 CBA). For 2003-2005 the company prorated these for short-service employees, calling the prior full payment an 'honest mistake' supported by a bare affidavit. The union grieved; voluntary arbitrators ordered restoration, affirmed by the CA.
cases.issue: Did full payment of 13th-month/bonus/leave benefits to short-service employees ripen into non-diminishable company practice under Art. 100?
cases.ruling: Yes — affirmed. CBA interpretation was settled by the arbitrators' finding (union's construction adopted). On practice: the company failed its burden (Art. 113(c)-style payroll proof absent); the 'mistake' defense collapsed on a bare affidavit without corroborating lapses in payroll procedure; and consistent voluntary grants over the CBA period ripened into practice — no fixed minimum number of years is required (2-, 3-, and 6-year precedents cited). Proration was ordered withdrawn.
cases.doctrine: (1) Voluntary, consistent benefit grants ripen into company practice protected by Art. 100 — no fixed minimum duration is required; (2) the employer bears the burden of proving payment according to law, and a 'mistake' defense needs corroboration beyond a bare affidavit.
cases.name: Arco Metal Products Co., Inc. v. SAMARM-NAFLU

cases.citation: G.R. No. 118506, 18 April 1997, First Division (Kapunan, J.)
cases.facts: Petitioners, hotel workers at La Campana, Cotabato City, discovered on inspection that their wages fell below minimum; the employer defended by valuing on-premises meals and lodging as deductible 'facilities.' The Labor Arbiter and NLRC credited the defense based on an accountant's certification and after-the-fact summaries.
cases.issue: May an employer deduct meals-and-lodging values from wages as 'facilities' without proof, and when are such benefits supplements instead?
cases.ruling: No — remanded for minimum-wage differentials. Facilities (Art. 97(f)) are deductible only on three conditions: (1) proof they are customarily furnished by the trade; (2) voluntary written acceptance by the employees; (3) fair and reasonable value. None was shown: the certification was self-serving, no payrolls/receipts supported it, values were not cost-based, and no real choice existed. Moreover the benefits were SUPPLEMENTS, not facilities — required residence/odd-hour availability served the employer's convenience (citing States Marine v. Cebu Seamen's, 7 SCRA 294: the purpose test).
cases.doctrine: (1) Facilities are deductible from wages only upon: trade-custom proof + voluntary written acceptance + fair reasonable value; (2) facilities vs supplements turns on PURPOSE — benefits furnished for the employer's convenience are non-deductible supplements.
cases.name: Mabeza v. NLRC

cases.citation: G.R. No. 131247, 25 January 1999, Third Division (Panganiban, J.)
cases.facts: The union claimed wage distortion because RA 6727's P25 increase and Cebu RTWPB WO-VI-02 raised Pay Classes 1-2 (Subic and Cebu) near or above Pay Class 3 (Cebu), while Cebu Pay Class 4 earners ended below Subic Pay Class 5 earners — invoking Art. 124 and the equal-pay principle.
cases.issue: Does regional implementation of wage orders create Art. 124 wage distortion, and do inter-regional pay inversions violate equal pay?
cases.ruling: No to both. Wage distortion has four elements: (1) an existing hierarchy of positions with corresponding salary rates; (2) a significant change in the salary rate of a lower pay class without a concomitant increase in higher classes; (3) elimination of the distinction embodied in the structure; (4) the same region. The petition failed element 2 as to differentials and element 4 throughout: 'establishment' (NWPC Guideline 1-1992) is a single fixed location, and RA 6727 deliberately differentiates by region — inter-regional disparity (higher-ranked Subic earners below lower-ranked Cebu earners) is the law's design under Arts. 99/122, not distortion and not an equal-pay violation.
cases.doctrine: (1) Wage distortion requires four elements (hierarchy; lower-level jump without higher-level match; elimination of distinction; SAME region/establishment); (2) regional wage-order implementation does not itself create distortion, and inter-regional pay disparity is RA 6727's design, not an equal-pay violation.

questions.prompt: A hotel hires (a) a front-office manager who directs 12 staff and whose hiring recommendations are always followed, (b) a maintenance foreman who assists the plant manager, exercises discretion over shifts, and spends 10% of his time on rank-and-file repairs, and (c) a messenger who reports daily to the office for assignments but spends most of the day delivering across the city on a fixed route with logbook entries. The hotel pays none of them overtime. Who is lawfully denied overtime pay, and under what tests?
questions.answerKey: (a) The manager meets all three Rule I Sec. 2(b) tests (manages a department, directs 2+ employees, hire/fire authority or weighted recommendations) — managerial employee, exempt. (b) The foreman fails 2(b) (not a department manager) but meets the Sec. 2(c) managerial-staff test (management-related work + discretion/independent judgment + assists a manager + within the 20% cap) — still exempt (Penaranda). (c) The messenger is covered: daily reporting + fixed route + logbooks make his hours determinable with reasonable certainty, so he is not field personnel (Art. 82; Rule I Sec. 2(f)) — overtime due, and job location alone never proves field-personnel status.
questions.explanation: Art. 82's exemptions are tested by actual duties under Rule I Sec. 2. Either the managerial-employee test (2(b): manage + direct 2+ + hire/fire weight) or the managerial-staff test (2(c): management-related + discretion + assist/specialized/special-tasks + 20% cap) removes the worker from Title I (Penaranda). Field personnel needs BOTH regular off-premises work AND hours not determinable with reasonable certainty — supervised, logged, scheduled field work fails the second test (Auto Bus).

questions.prompt: A worker (daily wage P800, 8-hour day) works 10 hours on a regular holiday that falls on his scheduled rest day. Separately, his supervisor lets him render 2 unauthorized overtime hours on an ordinary day, knowing about it. Compute/formulate the pay due for both situations and state whether the unauthorized hours are compensable.
questions.answerKey: Holiday-rest-day: first 8 hours at 260% (Rule IV Sec. 4: 200% + 30% of 200%) = P800 x 2.6 = P2,080; 2 OT hours at the first-8-hours rate + 30% (Art. 87 2nd sentence; Rule IV Sec. 5) = (P2,080 / 8) x 1.3 x 2 = P676; total P2,756. Unauthorized-but-known OT on an ordinary day IS compensable: 'suffered or permitted' work counts as hours worked (Art. 84(b); Rule I Sec. 4(c)) at the ordinary OT rate (hourly rate x 125%) — the remedy is discipline, not non-payment.
questions.explanation: Holiday-work rates compound: 200% base, 260% on a rest day, OT at the applicable first-8-hours rate x 130% (338% effective on a holiday-rest-day). Art. 84(b) makes known-but-unauthorized work compensable; Art. 88 separately bars offsetting it against other days' undertime.

questions.prompt: Maundy Thursday and Good Friday fall on Thursday-Friday this year. (a) An employee is absent without pay on Wednesday and does not work either holiday. (b) Another is absent without pay on Wednesday but works Maundy Thursday. (c) A third works Wednesday but the employer still withholds both holidays' pay 'because the shop was closed.' State who gets holiday pay and why.
questions.answerKey: (a) No holiday pay for either day: absence without pay on the day immediately preceding the FIRST of two successive regular holidays forfeits both (Rule IV Sec. 10). (b) Paid for Good Friday: working the first holiday earns the second (Sec. 10), plus 200% for the Maundy Thursday work (Sec. 4). (c) Paid for both: presence (or paid leave) on the preceding day entitles the worker to unworked-holiday pay (Sec. 6(a)); closure is not a ground to withhold — only Secretary-authorized business-reverses cessation is (Sec. 7(b)).
questions.explanation: Unworked-holiday pay turns on the immediately preceding day (present/paid-leave = paid; unpaid absence = may withhold), with Sec. 10's successive-holiday rule (absence before the first forfeits both unless the first is worked) and Sec. 7's narrow cessation exception. Worked holidays always earn the Sec. 4 rate regardless of prior absence.

questions.prompt: A restaurant collects a 10% service charge. Management distributes 85% to rank-and-file, keeps 15% for breakage and supervisor incentives, and counts the crew's service-charge share toward the latest wage-order increase. After a wage order raises the minimum, it also tells staff the service charge 'already covers' the increase. Identify every violation.
questions.answerKey: Three violations of Art. 96 as amended by RA 11360: (1) the 85/15 split is obsolete — 100% of collected service charges must go to covered workers except managerial employees; management may retain nothing; (2) service charges can never be credited toward minimum-wage compliance after an increase ('shall not be considered in determining compliance with the increased minimum wage'); (3) telling staff the charge 'covers' the increase restates violation (2). Distribution disputes go to the grievance mechanism, then DOLE conciliation.
questions.explanation: RA 11360 rewrote Art. 96: complete-and-equal distribution to covered workers (managerial employees excluded), a firewall between service charges and minimum-wage compliance, and a grievance-then-DOLE-conciliation dispute path. Pre-2019 85/15 materials state repealed law.

questions.prompt: After a new NCR wage order, a Manila company's Pay Grade 2 (P610) rises to the new P645 minimum while Pay Grade 3 stays at P650, obliterating a P40 gap that reflected skill and seniority. The company has no union. (a) Is there wage distortion? (b) What is the exact dispute procedure and does the P645 apply while it pends? (c) The Cebu branch pays P480 for the same grade — is that an equal-pay violation?
questions.answerKey: (a) Yes, prima facie: all four Prubankers elements appear (existing hierarchy; lower-level jump without higher-level match; elimination of the skill/seniority distinction; same region/establishment). (b) Without a union: negotiate, then NCMB conciliation (10 days), then the NLRC branch for compulsory arbitration — mandatory continuous hearings and decision within 20 calendar days of submission (Art. 124, 5th paragraph). The increase applies immediately: pendency never delays it (Art. 124, 6th paragraph). (c) No: regional differentiation is RA 6727's design (Arts. 99, 122); inter-regional disparity is neither distortion nor an equal-pay violation (Prubankers).
questions.explanation: Wage distortion = elimination/severe contraction of intentional quantitative differences based on skills, seniority, or logical differentiation. Art. 124 routes unionized disputes to grievance-then-voluntary-arbitration (10 days) and non-unionized ones to NCMB (10 days) then NLRC (20 days) — with immediate applicability throughout. Regional variation answers equal-pay objections.

questions.prompt: An employer deducts from wages: (a) SSS/PhilHealth/Pag-IBIG shares and withholding tax; (b) P500/month for 'cashier shortage insurance' from all cashiers' deposits without asking them; (c) union dues under a CBA check-off the employer signed; (d) meal values the company unilaterally priced, credited to meet minimum wage. Rule on each deduction.
questions.answerKey: (a) Lawful under Art. 113(c) (authorized by law). (b) Unlawful: deposits for loss/damage need a recognized trade practice or Secretary authority (Art. 114), and every draw-down needs prior hearing + clearly shown responsibility + actual amount only (Art. 115) — blanket advance deductions fail all three. (c) Lawful under Art. 113(b) (employer-recognized check-off). (d) Unlawful: facilities need trade-custom proof + voluntary written acceptance + fair reasonable value (Art. 97(f); Mabeza) — unilateral pricing fails conditions 2-3, and required-for-the-job meals are supplements (purpose test), not deductible at all.
questions.explanation: Art. 113's three exceptions (consented insurance, recognized/authorized check-off, law-or-Secretary authority) are exhaustive — unnamed deductions are illegal. Arts. 114-115 add the deposit-specific gates (recognized practice + heard + clearly shown + actual amount). Facility valuation needs the Mabeza trio, and employer-convenience benefits are non-deductible supplements.

questions.prompt: A sales supervisor (managerial employee) and a company driver (paid partly on task basis, partly fixed) each claim 13th-month pay. The company also computes rank-and-file 13th month on 'fixed salary + commissions + overtime.' A resigned clerk asks for proportionate 13th month at clearance. Rule on all four positions.
questions.answerKey: Supervisor: excluded — rank-and-file only (Revised Guidelines item 1). Driver: depends on classification — purely task-basis workers are exempt (item 2(d); David), but piece-rate workers are covered at 1/12 of total earnings, and mixed fixed+task workers follow the fixed component's coverage (task portion does not erase rank-and-file status for the fixed wage). Computation: commissions AND overtime must come out — commissions are not 'basic salary' (Boie-Takeda, voiding item 5(a) 2nd paragraph) and OT/premium/NSD/holiday pay/COLA are excluded unless integrated by agreement/practice. Resigned clerk: entitled proportionate (item 6), demandable upon separation.
questions.explanation: 13th-month coverage turns on rank-and-file status + >=1 month service, with the item 2(a)-(d) exemptions; the amount is >=1/12 of total BASIC salary (narrow base, Boie-Takeda-corrected); separation of any kind triggers proportionate payment; deadline December 24.

questions.prompt: Compare the six syllabus leaves (SIL, solo-parent parental, maternity, paternity, gynecological, VAWC) on: length, service requirement, payor/funding, and carryover/commutation. Then answer: a solo-parent mother of two (employed 8 months) gives birth to her third child — which leaves can she stack, and in what amounts?
questions.answerKey: SIL: 5 days, 12 months, employer-paid, commutes to cash (Art. 95; Rule V). Parental: 7 working days/yearly, 6 months, employer-paid, forfeitable/noncumulative (RA 11861 Sec. 7). Maternity: 105 days +15 solo-parent (+30 optional unpaid; 60 for miscarriage), SSS 3-contribution rule; SSS grant + employer advance/differential (RA 11210). Paternity: 7 days, married male, first 4 deliveries (RA 8187) — plus up to 7 allocable maternity days over and above (RA 11210 Sec. 6). Gynecological: 2 months at gross pay after surgery, 6-in-12 months (RA 9710 Sec. 18). VAWC: up to 10 days, stacks on all others, extendible via protection order (RA 9262 Sec. 43). The mother: 105 + 15 solo-parent maternity days (every pregnancy; legitimacy/civil status irrelevant), 7-day parental leave (8 months > 6-month requirement), and SIL only after 12 months — plus any VAWC leave on its own facts. She may also allocate up to 7 maternity days to the father/caregiver.
questions.explanation: The leave system is cumulative across laws (each leave has its own trigger) but internally disciplined (SIL commutes; parental forfeits; maternity allocates up to 7). Solo-parent status simultaneously unlocks RA 11861 leave and RA 11210's +15 days. VAWC leave is the only one expressly 'in addition to other paid leaves.'

questions.prompt: Rico is hired as a delivery rider paid per parcel delivered ('pakyaw'). He reports to the depot each morning for route assignments, follows a fixed delivery sequence, logs every parcel in the company app, and returns each evening for accounting. After two years without holiday pay, SIL pay, or 13th-month pay, he files money claims. The company argues: (1) pakyaw workers are not employees; (2) riders are field personnel; (3) per-parcel workers cannot claim any of the three benefits. Resolve each argument.
questions.answerKey: Rico is an employee: under David v. Macasio, pakyaw is only a pay method under Arts. 97 and 101, and control — morning route assignments, a fixed delivery sequence, app logs, and evening accounting — establishes employment under the four-fold test. He is not field personnel under Art. 82, because his hours can be determined with reasonable certainty from that supervised routine; like the supervised workers in David and Auto Bus, the task-basis phrases in Rules I, IV, and V are read with 'field personnel' by ejusdem generis and do not exclude him. He is therefore entitled to holiday pay under Art. 94 and, having rendered over a year of service, to 5-day SIL pay under Art. 95, commutable to cash. But his 13th-month claim fails: PD 851, Sec. 3(e) and Revised Guidelines item 2(d) exempt workers paid on purely task basis absolutely, with no field-personnel qualifier (David). In short, company arguments (1) and (2) fail, while argument (3) is only half-right — it defeats the 13th-month claim alone.

hints.issue: Employment status of a pakyaw rider + entitlement to holiday pay, SIL pay, and 13th-month pay despite non-time pay and field work.
hints.rule: Art. 97/101 (pakyaw is a pay method); Art. 82 + Rules I/IV/V (field-personnel test; ejusdem generis reading of task-basis phrases — David, Auto Bus, Serrano); Arts. 94/95 (holiday/SIL pay); PD 851 Sec. 3(e) / Guidelines item 2(d) (absolute task-basis exemption from 13th-month pay — David).
hints.application: Test control first (assignments, sequence, app logs, accounting = supervision + determinable hours, so not field personnel) before applying each benefit's own rule; note the 13th-month rule cuts the opposite way from the other two.
hints.conclusion: Employee, entitled to holiday and SIL pay, but not 13th-month pay.

questions.prompt: For six straight years, a company paid all employees — including those hired mid-year — a full December 'loyalty bonus' equal to one month's salary, on top of 13th-month pay. This year, citing losses, it prorates the bonus by months served and scraps it entirely for employees with under 6 months. Affected employees invoke Art. 100. The company counters that bonuses are gratuitous, losses justify the cut, and the prior payments were 'computation errors.' Resolve the dispute.
questions.answerKey: The full loyalty bonus is enforceable as company practice under Art. 100. Six years of voluntary, consistent full-month grants — even to employees hired mid-year — ripen into practice under Arco Metal, which requires no fixed minimum number of years, so the gratuity defense fails. The losses defense fails too, since business losses are not an Art. 100 exception. The 'computation error' defense fails on burden of proof: the employer must prove payment according to law, and Arco Metal rejects a bare mistake claim without corroborating payroll-procedure evidence. Because the bonus was paid on top of 13th-month pay, the PD 851, Sec. 2 and Guidelines item 2(b) 'already paying' credit does not absorb it — only payments meeting or exceeding 1/12 of basic salary count, and any shortfall must be topped up. The proration and the under-6-months cutoff are therefore void diminutions; the full bonus stands.

hints.issue: Whether a repeatedly paid full loyalty bonus ripened into non-diminishable company practice under Art. 100, and who bears the burden on the 'error' and 'losses' defenses.
hints.rule: Art. 97(f) (bonus as gratuity vs wage); Art. 100 (non-diminution); Arco Metal (voluntary consistent grants + no fixed minimum years + employer burden + corroborated-mistake requirement); PD 851 Sec. 2 / Guidelines item 2(b) ('already paying' credit rules).
hints.application: Test each defense: gratuity yields to ripened practice; losses are not an Art. 100 exception (distinguish authorized-cause wage-order/distressed exemptions); 'error' needs corroboration beyond allegation; check whether the bonus was already creditable against 13th-month obligations.
hints.conclusion: Full bonus enforceable as company practice; proration and scrapping void as diminution.

flashcards.front: Art. 82: name the seven groups EXCLUDED from Title I (hours/rest/holidays/SIL) coverage.
flashcards.back: Government employees; managerial employees; field personnel; family members dependent on the employer; domestic helpers; persons in personal service of another; workers paid by results (per Secretary regulations).

flashcards.front: Field personnel test (Art. 82 + Rule I Sec. 2(f)): what two elements must BOTH be present?
flashcards.back: (1) Non-agricultural employee regularly performing duties AWAY from the principal/branch office; AND (2) actual hours of work in the field CANNOT be determined with reasonable certainty. Supervised/logged field work (Auto Bus driver, David butcher) fails element 2.

flashcards.front: State the overtime and premium rate ladder: ordinary OT; rest-day/special-holiday first 8 hours; special holiday on rest day; regular holiday; regular holiday on rest day; OT on a regular-holiday rest day.
flashcards.back: Ordinary OT 125%; rest-day/special-holiday 130% (OT on them: that rate x 130%); special-on-rest-day 150%; regular holiday 200%; regular-on-rest-day 260%; OT on regular-holiday-rest-day 260% x 130% = 338%. (Arts. 87, 93; Rule I Sec. 9; Rule IV Secs. 4-5.)

flashcards.front: Hours worked (Art. 84): the two tests + the short-rest rule. Which common periods are compensable vs not?
flashcards.back: (a) Required to be on duty/at a prescribed place; OR (b) suffered/permitted to work. Short rest periods count as hours worked. Compensable: waiting integral to work, confined on-call, necessary after-hours work known to supervisor, required travel, 5-20 min coffee breaks, shortened (<60 min) meals. Not: genuine 60-min meal, free-to-leave breaks, ordinary commute, truly voluntary off-hours lectures with no productive work (Rule I Secs. 3-7).

flashcards.front: CWW (DA 02-2004): 3 recognition conditions + 2 hard OT ceilings + the diminution rule.
flashcards.back: Conditions: majority voluntary agreement; OSHS certification where hazardous; DOLE notice. Ceilings: OT premium always due past 12 hours/day or 48 hours/week. No diminution from adoption — and reverting to 8 hours is NOT diminution. Excluded: construction, health services, heavy manual labor, OSHS-exceeding exposures.

flashcards.front: Art. 96 as amended by RA 11360: who gets service charges, and what is the minimum-wage firewall?
flashcards.back: 100% to covered workers except managerial employees (85/15 split repealed). Service charges can NEVER be credited toward minimum-wage compliance after a wage increase. Disputes: grievance mechanism, then DOLE conciliation.

flashcards.front: Art. 97(f) 'wage': give the definition's three exam extensions (designation, timing, facilities) + the commissions and bonus rules.
flashcards.back: Covers ALL remuneration however designated (time/task/piece/COMMISSION); for work done OR TO BE DONE; includes fair value of facilities with NO employer profit. Commissions are wages (Art. 97(f)) but NOT 13th-month 'basic salary' (Boie-Takeda). Bonus is gratuitous unless promised (contract/CBA) or ripened into practice (Art. 100; Arco Metal).

flashcards.front: Minimum-wage machinery: who fixes rates, the 15-10-60 sequence, and where to verify the current rate (and why no peso figure is stated).
flashcards.back: RTWPBs fix regional rates via wage orders (Art. 99/122(b)) within NWPC guidelines; NWPC = policy + review + appeals. Effectivity 15 days after complete regional publication; appeal to NWPC within 10 calendar days; NWPC decides within 60; appeal does not stay unless bonded (Art. 123). Verify on NWPC/RTWPB official postings — rates vary by region/order, so no single national peso figure exists.

flashcards.front: Wage distortion (Art. 124): definition + Prubankers' four elements + both dispute tracks and pendency effect.
flashcards.back: Increase in prescribed rates eliminating/severely contracting intentional quantitative differences based on skills, seniority, or logical differentiation. Elements: existing hierarchy; lower-level jump without higher-level match; elimination of distinction; SAME region. Union: negotiate -> grievance -> voluntary arbitration (10 days). No union: NCMB conciliation (10 days) -> NLRC compulsory arbitration (20 days). Pendency never delays the increase.

flashcards.front: Art. 113: the only three lawful wage deductions. What test applies to everything else?
flashcards.back: (a) Consented insurance premiums advanced by the employer; (b) union-dues check-off recognized or individually authorized in writing; (c) deductions authorized by law (SSS/PhilHealth/Pag-IBIG/tax) or Secretary regulations. Everything else is ILLEGAL unless the employer names its (a)/(b)/(c) authority; facility values additionally need trade custom + written acceptance + fair value (Mabeza).

flashcards.front: 13th-month pay: coverage, minimum amount, base exclusions, deadline, and the separated-employee rule.
flashcards.back: All rank-and-file with >=1 month service (managerial, government, household, purely commission/boundary/task excluded; piece-rate covered). Minimum 1/12 of total BASIC salary — commissions (Boie-Takeda), OT, premium, NSD, holiday pay, COLA excluded unless integrated. Deadline December 24. Any separation: proportionate 13th month demandable at separation.

flashcards.front: SIL (Art. 95): floor, service rule, the three non-applicabilities, and commutation — plus who else is covered by case law.
flashcards.back: 5 days with pay yearly after 12 months (continuous or broken, incl. authorized absences/paid holidays). Not applicable to: already-enjoying-equivalent, >=5-day vacation leave holders, <10-employee or Secretary-exempted establishments. Unused SIL commutes to cash (even on separation, prorated). Pakyaw/task and commission workers covered unless field personnel (David, Auto Bus).

flashcards.front: Solo-parent parental leave (current RA 11861 text): length, service, carryover, sector — and the syllabus citation trap.
flashcards.back: 7 WORKING days/year with pay, after 6 months service, FORFEITABLE and NONCUMULATIVE, public AND private, regardless of status. Trap: RA 8972 has only Secs. 1-17 — there is NO Sec. 20 (syllabus citation erroneous); current text is RA 11861 Sec. 7 amending RA 8972 Sec. 8.

flashcards.front: Maternity (RA 11210) ladder: 105/60/30/15/7 — what each number means, plus funding mechanics.
flashcards.back: 105 days live birth (+15 solo-parent; 60 miscarriage/emergency termination; +30 optional unpaid). SSS member + 3 contributions in prior 12 months; employer advances within 30 days, SSS reimburses 100%, employer pays differential unless exempt (distressed, retail/service <=10, micro <=P3M, already-providing). Up to 7 days allocable to father/caregiver, over and above RA 8187. Every pregnancy; legitimacy/civil status/delivery mode irrelevant.

flashcards.front: Paternity (RA 8187) vs maternity allocation vs gynecological (RA 9710) vs VAWC (RA 9262): trigger, length, key limiter each.
flashcards.back: Paternity: married male, legitimate cohabiting spouse's delivery (incl. miscarriage), 7 days, first 4 deliveries. Allocation: any father/partner/relative, up to 7 maternity days, over and above paternity. Gynecological: female, SURGERY for gynecological disorder, 2 months at gross pay, 6-in-12 months service. VAWC: victim, up to 10 days paid, stacks on ALL other leaves, extendible via protection order; assisting co-employees protected.

flashcards.front: Apprentice vs learner vs PWD worker: occupation, period, wage floor, agreement, and the conversion/commitment rule.
flashcards.back: Apprentice: highly-technical industry + approved occupation, >3 months training + theory, <=6 months, >=75% minimum (Art. 61; unpaid only if school-required + Secretary-authorized, Art. 72). Learner: semi-skilled non-apprenticeable, <=3 months, >=75% (time) / 100% (piece, Art. 76), hire-commitment + 2-month auto-regularization if cut short (Art. 75). PWD: Art. 80 agreement (>=75%), bridge to apprentice/learner chapters via Art. 81; qualified PWDs get equal terms/pay (RA 7277 Sec. 5).
